The Erasmus Experiment has proven that magnetospheric ULF wave motions can be detected
firsthand by a navigating spacecraft as more than just dimensional changes, but rather
as tangible vibrations that can be heard through sound waves. This experiment has shown
that the frequencies and amplitudes of these sound waves correspond to the wave
magnitude spectra and temporal variations observed by the Freja satellite. Although the
sound example given is based on simulated data, real-spacecraft sound recordings are
highly anticipated for the upcoming MMS mission, which will convert the vibrations
encountered by the mission into audible waves.

This research focuses on a class of rotating, charged, asymptotically flat black holes that incorporate a non-linear electromagnetic component described by a logarithmic relationship. We explore how the presence of a non-linear electromagnetic field influences the black hole's physical characteristics. In addition to establishing the complete mass-charge relationship for these black holes, we demonstrated that they comply with the first law of thermodynamics. We have explored how the non-linear electromagnetic coupling affects temperature, specific heat, and entropy. We have conducted extensive computational studies for these thermodynamic properties under various extreme conditions. The results illustrate how the non-linear electromagnetic coupling impacts thermodynamic quantities. It's observed that these black holes exhibit adiabatic behavior at specific temperature and charge configurations. The findings of this research can be extended to a broader range of electromagnetic non-linearities, offering fresh perspectives on the thermodynamics of rotating black holes.

In machine learning representation, various methods have been employed to enhance the processing capabilities of associated data. The way text data is represented significantly influences performance in tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, sentiment analysis, and information extraction for specific domains. A comprehensive framework for representing text data is presented, utilizing descriptive memory concepts to model intricate text patterns. This method utilizes a DeSM-based text representation scheme to achieve enhanced representation learning outcomes for diverse NLP tasks. Furthermore, a hybrid method for pretraining transformers using descriptive memory concepts and language models is introduced, demonstrating improved performance using real-world text data. Experiments were conducted on multiple NLP tasks, showcasing the superiority of the proposed descriptive memory-based approach compared to established state-of-the-art and state-of-the-moment baselines.

We establish that every (universal) CAR algebra can be constructed as the result of applying a morphism to a universal CCR algebra, and this morphism can be defined using a specific Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra. Notably, our approach differs from the conventional method of constructing the CAR from the CCR by incorporating creation and annihilation operators. The novel technique involves defining operator flows that map CCR operators to CAR operators, and we utilize the KMS state of the Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra to define an expectation state within both the CCR and CAR algebras, while also establishing that both algebras are fully dense subalgebras within the respective Hilbert space. Additionally, our study includes an investigation of the representation theory of the CAR algebra.

This paper introduces a refined, step-by-step syntactic framework for Isabelle/ZK GP 2, building on the author's prior work. A small-step operational semantics in Isabelle/FP, along with soundness and fullness proofs, are also presented. These concepts are best illustrated through the use case of a distributed cache system.

We analyze possible outcomes of photoevaporation from the TW Hydrae young disk as observed at 88 GHz with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). If we assume that the disk has a structural break of 30 AU or more from its outer portion as seen in observations, then we expect to see typically four to six bright rings or gaps in the ALMA image. However, if the disk has a more compact outer portion (less than 30 AU from its outer portion as seen in observations) then we would see typically three to five distinct areas within the disk's CO emission. These areas would be shaped by how gas and dust behave within the disk and would be influenced by how strongly the outer disk is affected by photoevaporation. However, if the disk's outer portion as seen in observations is expanded or contracted by a small amount, then the areas within the disk's CO emission would also need to be correspondingly adjusted. Furthermore, our model suggests that future, high-resolution radio observations could easily distinguish between these areas within the disk's CO emission and would therefore be able to confirm or deny certain models of how the disk is behaving.

We address the factorization of specific polynomial variants by developing new solutions for expressions involving Chebyshev polynomials of the third and fourth kinds. Our proof method leverages previous work by Wolfram on factorizing variants of Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kinds. Additionally, we establish that minimal polynomials with higher degree factors are insufficient to factor certain Chebyshev polynomial variants, which necessitates exploring alternative methods.

This research proposes an innovative method of protection and classification for transient phenomena in only one section of a distribution network that employs two-core load tap changers with automatic regulation. Since these devices are located near the point of common coupling and close to the load, the earth current flows through them during earth faults. The proposed system utilizes the current and voltage measurements on only one side to identify and categorize fault types at the tap changer. The development of this system was prompted by the limitations of conventional systems that necessitate separate measurement points for phase and earth currents and are incapable of distinguishing between earth faults and tapping malfunctions. The proposed system employs an adaptive neural network with detection and classification modules to determine whether a fault has occurred and, if so, to identify the type of fault. The system also includes automatic and intelligent features such as testing, false alarms suppression, and battery charging control. The results of simulation and real-world testing confirm the system's efficacy. The testing showed that the system can accurately detect and classify faults with an overall root mean square square error of 0.0836 and a correlation coefficient of 0.9968.

In molecular dynamics simulations of vapor-liquid coexistence, generating data for phase diagram creation from Monte Carlo simulations can be computationally expensive due to the large amount of data generated, leading to high data storage and analysis costs. To address this issue, we investigate how to efficiently transmit the generated data, specifically multi-partite structures, over mmWave links with high transmission speeds and efficient networks. Firstly, we evaluate the performance of conventional mmWave multicasting using one wavevector per group and discover that this approach is limited by the minimum number of transmitters, which is the major factor hindering good performance. Secondly, we propose a novel encoding method, called hybrid encoding, that uses a combination of one-way and two-way encoding principles. This method is expected to take full advantage of the transmission capabilities, resulting in improved performance by a factor of the minimum number of transmitters. Finally, we compared our method with the conventional encoding method, and the results showed that the proposed hybrid encoding method can achieve a 56% lower bandwidth when encoding 8-group data and a 41% shorter time is required to achieve the same bandwidth as conventional encoding method when encoding data using 8 transmitters.

A group's 'rank' is defined as the maximum rank of all irreducible representations. Given this definition, we can establish that a near-exponential growth pattern in the number of irreducible representations of a group G, as the rank increases, implies that G has near-exponential growth in its orbit counting under conjugation. Additionally, this near-exponential growth pattern can be translated to a near-exponential growth pattern in the number of G's subgroups as the rank increases. Furthermore, this near-exponential growth pattern can be utilized to prove that a near-exponential growth pattern in the number of irreducible representations of a group G implies that G has near-exponential growth in its Bruhat-Tits building. However, this near-exponential growth pattern holds one significant limitation: it is inapplicable to groups of algebraic type.

We analyze the asymptotic stability of a star-shaped network of infinitely thin and infinitely flexible bars, where each node has three branches and one point of attachment. By applying Hennison's technique in the context of Lyapunov's second method, we identify the long-term dynamics of this system. We observe that in addition to standard behaviors like exponential decay, we also find evidence of algebraic decay, a phenomenon that may be attributed to the system's internal dynamics near its equilibrium state.

For the creation of artificial radioactive elements in advanced reactor experiments, accurate knowledge of nuclear mass is essential. A key challenge lies in determining the masses of unstable, heavy isotopes, which current physics models cannot adequately predict. By utilizing a novel machine learning technique known as the all-encompassing neural network, we have developed a tool to calculate nuclear mass using stable, nearby data points as inputs. This tool not only allows for precise prediction of mass but also assesses associated uncertainty. Importantly, our results indicate that the machine learning model can achieve an uncertainty of less than 120 keV for the mass of heavily neutron-rich, isotopes - a margin that is sufficient for the creation of radioactive elements in reactor experiments. Furthermore, by studying random realizations of known nuclear mass distributions, we have confirmed that the calculated uncertainty is an accurate representation of uncertainty. Additionally, the mass of 60 elements, along with associated uncertainties, has been calculated using our model, which is available for public download at www.nucml.net.

Superconducting qubit performance is constrained by dielectric loss, which must be minimized to achieve practical operation frequencies, possibly reaching the phonon lifetime limit to be reliable in the quantum regime. Researchers have developed a method to measure dielectric loss in sapphire, combining it with a micro-machined cavity to reach an astonishing sensitivity of parts-per-billion, a level that has not been previously attained. By utilizing this technique, the dielectric loss of various sapphire materials was examined, yielding the world's lowest dielectric loss for 0.5% type 1100-hynd 0.5 mm sapphire, with a cut-loss frequency of 11.8 GHz. Furthermore, the study's findings highlight the importance of using high-purity sapphire in the development of quantum classically-synchronized superconducting qubits. It has also shown that dielectric loss can be accurately measured over a broad frequency range, ranging from 2 to 12 GHz, through a technique that uses transmission coefficient data along with genetic least-squares fitting of various coupling models. This method has the ability to resolve cut-off frequency differences of just 10 kHz and can predict transmission coefficients with an accuracy of $10^{-5}$ at high magnification.

Theories involving interactions between electromagnetic fields and mechanical movements are well-established, yet practical applications often demonstrate more complex relationships than initially anticipated. This research proposes a theoretical framework for mechanical resonance based on the symmetry between Maxwell's equations and the equations of motion, where both systems share a common polarization. By analyzing this polarization, the study develops an original model for coupled electromagnetic and mechanical phenomena and employs it to investigate the movement of a mirror in response to laser irradiation, where the mirror's oscillations produce unique variations in phase and amplitude. This effect could potentially be exploited to develop highly precise and controlled optical manipulation techniques.

This paper introduces a computationally efficient solution technique for the Lagrangian relaxation of two-stage robust optimization problems where variables take binary values. The challenge of computational complexity in stage one, resulting from binary variables and uncertain parameters, is mitigated by applying an innovative dual approach. First, a lower bound for the optimal objective value is calculated by solving a simplified problem obtained through Lagrangian relaxation. Then, a Lagrangian dual problem is formed using the constraints, and its solution yields feasible solutions for the original problem. By iterating this process, the optimal solution is identified. The technique is demonstrated through the application to robust maximum-cut problem and robust clique-cover problem, with empirical results showcasing its effectiveness in finding accurate solutions quickly, even for large parametric problems.

The diverse city of Beijing faces significant social disparities.  This issue can be explored with the help of a comprehensive dataset that contains multiple types of data such as regional distributions, demographic information, transportation patterns, as well as air quality data.  This dataset was designed to facilitate the study of urban inequality, thereby allowing researchers to develop more effective solutions to address related problems.  The purpose of this paper is to present a comprehensive dataset known as H4M/Beijing that is intended to support sustainable and equitable urban development.  The paper discusses various aspects of this dataset, including its creation, composition, formatting, data characteristics, preprocessing techniques, labeling efforts, data splits, and potential applications.  The research community is invited to use this dataset for a variety of purposes such as understanding socioeconomic trends and developing more effective solutions to address urban inequality.

Over the past decade, visual analytics has emerged as a pivotal approach for tackling 'big data,' allowing users to harness the potential of computational visualization to gain insights that might elude them without the aid of a visual representation. However, the intricacies involved in crafting effective visualizations that uncover hidden patterns in data are still shrouded in complexity, largely due to the fragmented state of current visual design patterns and the scarcity of interactive tools that facilitate exploration. In response to these challenges, our study introduces a unified framework for visual design, incorporating principles of visual encoding and semantic mapping. Furthermore, building upon this framework, we develop DVDE, a visual design-driven tool that enables the interactive exploration of multi-variable data sets by leveraging'sensitivity analysis,' which uncovers correlations among variables, and 'visual design,' which allows users to incorporate new visual elements to expose hidden patterns in the data. Such innovative capabilities differentiate DVDE from numerous commercial and academic tools, providing users with the opportunity to gain fresh and unique insights from the data. Through thorough evaluations and case studies, including an in-depth analysis of NASA's multi-heliospheric Sun Earth Connection Observations, we establish that DVDE facilitates fresh and precise insights that cannot be discerned with the aid of a conventional visualization.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have led to their increasing adoption in real-world systems from network management to malware analysis, largely due to their ability to interpret real-world data through interconnected structures. The field of deep neural networks, including GNNs, is undergoing rapid evolution with numerous research papers being published annually. Building upon this momentum, this research aims to identify factors contributing to the survival of GNN-based models by surveying the literature and examining the relevance of their underlying components, enabling the creation of GNNs that can effectively adapt to graph domains. A GNN-based assessment framework, comprising both classification and link prediction tasks, was utilized to analyze the influence of 16 essential features, including hyperparameters and transfer learning techniques, on these models. The results revealed that using transfer learning with a linear adapter yields superior outcomes compared to other methods, highlighting adjustments to linear adapters as a key factor for improving GNN model resilience. The research also pinpointed specific hyperparameters and transfer learning approaches contributing to these models' success. The comprehensive analysis, evaluation, and comparison of features enabled the identification of best practices for developing robust GNNs and revealed opportunities for future research to address challenges within the field.

A collaborative filtering system predicts user preferences by identifying patterns in user behavior. One effective method for doing so is to analyze users who share similar interests, even without knowing the actual labels. For instance, the items that one user likes and another user has liked can help forecast which items the first user will like next. At its core, the challenge of user collaboration boils down to a statistical problem where users and their interests are considered random variables with unknown distributions. A model that treats users and items as units that share latent characteristics through a coefficient matrix, similar to how a certain method treats users and news articles as units that share common themes through a coefficient matrix, is presented. Although the model has the ability to accurately forecast how users will interact with certain items, it also allows for calculations that predict which groups of users will share similar interests given certain items, and it also allows for calculations that predict which groups of users will share similar interests given item labels. Furthermore, the accuracy of forecasts from the model is compared to those of other systems on a number of datasets.

We present a straightforward proof of a novel separation between $\ell_1$ and Hamming norms, which has significant implications for data streams. Unlike previous approaches that relied on Gaussian methods with intricate mathematical foundations, our proof is easily accessible and requires no specialized knowledge. This result has substantial practical applications, enabling more efficient linear hash functions in data streams.

We investigate the momentum dependence of the static magnetic susceptibility of Heisenberg magnets within the paramagnetic phase, building on the momentum-dependent nonlinear sigma model and its associated $1/N$ expansion. A novel method is employed to analyze the model's large momentum behavior, and the results show that the momentum dependence of the magnetic susceptibility is significant at large momenta. Accounting for this phenomenon yields a more accurate calculation of the critical exponents within the $3d$ nonlinear sigma model with a $6-\phi$ universality class. The corresponding value of the exponents is found to be $\frac{g_N\epsilon^{-1}}{2}=\frac{1.5687}{\epsilon}+0.5498$, where $\epsilon$ approximates $1.5738$ for $O(N)$ scalar field theory. The study demonstrates that the critical exponents are influenced by the momentum-dependent structure of the magnetic susceptibility in $3d$ Heisenberg magnets.

The development of reliable and efficient single atom trapping, manipulation, and detection techniques is crucial to realizing applications of single atoms, including quantum computing and sensing. We present a method to achieve these procedures by utilizing multi-grating eigenstates to create an attractive atom-grating potential. This approach can produce a trap at the intersection of multiple gratings, providing a confined environment for atom confinement. However, this method has a critical requirement - an array of at least six gratings. Although this may seem complicated, our method has the advantage of using only one atomic isomer, and it does not necessitate the use of complicate optical control techniques. Furthermore, we explored the possibilities of using an all-optical method to create an attractive potential between atoms and gratings. This technique could lead to the development of compact devices capable of trapping, manipulating, and detecting single atoms.

In an invariant time-reversal environment, researchers investigate the conductance of a two-dimensional system with interaction and disorder, which exhibits linear and nonlinear Hall conductance. The results demonstrate that if a system is in a ground state that is unperturbed by time-reversal, its linear Hall conductance will remain unchanged by interactions, whereas the nonlinear Hall conductance will be directly proportional to the amount of disorder. The findings also include zero-temperature and zero-charge density relationships for nonlinear Hall conductance in varying environments. Additionally, researchers derived an exact method for calculating conductivity in two-dimensional systems with interaction and disorder, which can be applied to any system, including ones under stress, in a non-uniform state, with spin rotation symmetry breaking. The method for two-dimensional systems with interaction and disorder is different from those previously established for one-dimensional systems.

The Second COVID-19 surge led to a severe Meso-American Oxygen shortage resulting in unnecessary patient deaths. To prevent similar crises during future pandemics, Medical Ventilation Centers must effectively plan their operations in advance to meet expected patient demands. In this study, we employ the direct transcription approach to model dual-patient ventilation and optimize a ventilation center's capacity expansion to a specified future capacity, mimicking the requirements of dual-patient anesthesia during the COVID-19 pandemic. Anesthesia equipment cannot be used for both patients at the same time, thus patients share the equipment. We are the first to develop a procedure for optimizing a ventilation center's expansion to its future capacity while considering the equipment usage restrictions. Our proposed method, also known as sequential optimal expansion, allows for sequential and successful patient deinstallations of anesthesological equipment at the end of their treatment, yielding a significantly improved (up to 35\%) equipment usage and a reduced number of installations needed for the same number of patients. Additionally, we employ a novel numerical approach that combines direct transcription with a generalized derivative-based augmented Lagrangian method for solving complementarity problems, yielding successful results for a variety of examples.

A rational mapping from the Riemann sphere to itself is considered bicritical if it has precisely two points in its orbit under iteration, excluding the point at infinity. We provide a detailed description of the regions in the parameter space where such maps exhibit certain behavior: their deck groups change in composition, size, or structure as they map certain non-infinite points to each other. Our analysis involves identifying the boundaries where such changes occur and examining the patterns in the resulting regions, especially for maps that have a particular branch pattern associated with "wild" behavior.

Two-dimensional semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenides have drawn a lot of interest due to their unique properties and potential to be used in high-speed electronic devices. However, whether these 2D semiconductors can also facilitate stable, threshold-voltage-adjustable gate contacts remains unclear. In order to address this, the work function of Mo and W dichalcogenides with different layers was examined using techniques such as first-principles calculations, which were accompanied by gas-phase photoemission and transport measurements. The results from these experiments indicate that work functions of these materials can be operated on, which indicates the feasibility of implementing Mo and W dichalcogenides in gate contacts that can be adjusted electronically.

A widely used technique for adjusting code is through delta lenses, combining the benefits of monotonic and anti-monotonic transformations via a form of fusion. This technique has seen applications in code refactoring, programming education, and the development of IDE tools. Our research reveals that the basic delta lens framework can be directly applied to a broad range of supervised machine learning algorithms used in computer-assisted programming. These algorithms typically rely on a model and target code pair to calculate adjustments, similar to how delta lenses utilize a model and target code triple. We discuss the benefits of incorporating the delta lens formalism into this field, along with challenges that arise from the unique characteristics of the domain and potential solutions to overcome these obstacles.

We establish a new uniform version of the stationary phase formula under the low smoothness condition of H\"older continuity of $\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$. Moreover, it can be demonstrated that if the local model of a phase function is an ellipsoid, the initial term in the expansion of the phase function determines the asymptotic behavior of the integral, while the second term may be omitted. This outcome also facilitates a new expression for the uniform stationary phase formula with the low smoothness condition of H\"older continuity of $\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$.

A crucial challenge in rarefied gas physics concerns determining the steady-state gas flow between two evenly scaled regions with reflective boundaries, where particles primarily interact via elastic collisions. To resolve this problem, a iterative solution algorithm is proposed, combining an asymptotic solution with a linear correction scheme, similar to the approach developed by Prezzi, Sisi, and Varilla. Through analysis, it's shown that this algorithm shares the same convergence properties as the original solution algorithm, yet with a significantly reduced iteration count. Specifically, it's estimated that the algorithm requires around 70 iterations to achieve a relative error of $10^{-7}$. To support this claim, numerical experiments using Python's numpy and scipy libraries are presented.

The Horizon-10T collaboration reported a series of large loss-lepton events, prompting an analysis to explore potential relationships with cosmic phenomena and astrophysical sources. A specific observation of these events matching a specific distribution of energy and time could be linked to a cosmic ray with properties linked to an active galactic nucleus event observed by an experiment. Furthermore, these events might be the result of massive quark clusters colliding with the Earth's atmosphere, a hypothesis that can be studied using a specific distribution of energy and momentum known as the HEEP signature. A multi-modal analysis of these events, combining data from both Horizon-10T and HEEP, indicates a possible connection to a massive, charged particle with electric and magnetic charges. This particle, known as a monopole, is consistent with a specific mass range that can explain the observed distribution of energy clusters. A variety of simulations have been performed to study the properties of these massive quark clusters, confirming their potential connection to a massive, charged particle with distinct electric and magnetic properties.

The latest CMS results for the Higgs-like boson's two photon decay, based on 25.7 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV, are presented. The observed signal exhibits a combined significance of 6.1 standard deviations. The anticipated two photon decay of the 125 GeV Higgs boson, as predicted by the Standard Model, is closely aligned with the observed data, particularly in terms of its spin-parity characteristics. Additionally, the outcome is inconsistent with findings from the Higgs-Strangelet Pair and the Z boson's two photon decay modes.

We introduce a concept for the p-divisibility transposition of the Fourier coefficients 
of Siegel modular functions. This concept complements the Wilton result on p-divisibility for the Ramanujan $\tau$-function.

For a finite sequence of positive integers, denoted by $\boldsymbol{i}$, this thesis explores maps with a specific characteristic - they map an $n$-dimensional space onto a $b$-dimensional space while contracting dimensions by $c_1, \dots,c_n$ across their fibres, with each $c_i$ equal to or exceeding $1$. The main focus is on determining a precise sequence of these fibres, $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{i})$, such that the resulting map is a fibre bundle. The initial findings from this research relate to the specific case where all $c_i$ are $1$, resulting in fibre sequences. Additionally, statements regarding the dimensionality of resulting spaces, $\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(0)$ and $\bigcap_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(I_i)$, where $I_i$ are intervals, have also been identified.

The isospin-dependent Pauli principle exhibits a distinct macroscopic effect in two-dimensional particle systems, leading to a structural anomaly in the phase diagram. To illustrate this, we examine the two-dimensional particle systems of neutrons and protons inside atomic nuclei, known as isotope lattices, to identify an unusual phase transition that arises from the superposition of two underlying phase transitions, one associated with the Fermi gas critical density and another with the ordering of magnetic dipole moments. Furthermore, we explore other two-dimensional particle systems that display this characteristic "isospin-dependent order-disorder" phase transition, including those with complex spin interactions, such as the BCS model and the resonating-valence-bond state, the cluster model, and the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on a square lattice. Additionally, we discuss possible experimental manifestations of this phase anomaly in nucleons.

This initial chapter provides a fundamental understanding of predicting dynamic matrix problems via Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN). In this foundational book, we introduce the theory and implementation of ZNN for forecasting tasks. Following an introduction to ZNN's theory, the chapter focuses on the practical applications of this method for predicting tasks, including a detailed explanation of the involved problems, the ZNN design process, and the steps for constructing ZNN models. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of ZNN for predicting tasks and explore the advantages of this approach before concluding with a look at the potential future directions of ZNN in predicting tasks.

The success of edge computing in image classification benefits from advanced
neural networks with efficient and robust core processing capabilities. The
neural structure of these algorithms resembles the biological visual system of
animals, with a distinct pattern of rod cells and cone cells in the retina.
The rod cells detect basic changes while the cone cells identify essential
details. A newly proposed classification system consists of rod cells and cone
cells, which not only mimics the retina but also utilizes a local-to-global
processing strategy to save computational resources and reduce power
consumption. The experiments show that the newly designed structure achieves
higher accuracy and is more resistant to noise than other popular techniques.

In wide-field X-ray observatory projects like e-ASTROGATE/ARC and CUTE, next-generation X-ray telescopes must cover a wide range of fields, from 10 to 100 square degrees in a single point, with diffraction limits below 1 keV below. To achieve this goal, the designs of the X-ray optics, including new methods for altering the wavelength dependence, are discussed. These methods involve altering the curvature of individual shell segments in a shell-type X-ray telescope or using a flat, rotating reflector surface. By adjusting either the radius of curvature of individual shell segments or the length of a flat segment in a fully folded design, the overall wavelength dependence of an X-ray optical system can be altered. Various parameter studies in a four-section test dish demonstrated that an X-ray optical system with a wavelength of 0.15 nm instead of 0.2 nm could be achieved using a moderate curvature variation, without significantly impacting other optical properties. Similarly, an fully folded design using 84 segments shows that using 120 segments instead of 84, with corresponding adjustments to segment length, allows an X-ray optical system with a wavelength of 0.15 nm instead of 0.2 nm at the same optical distance, without significantly altering other optical properties. Simulations of the wide-field X-ray observatory in a 10-degree circular field show that a four-section dish with 120 segments in a fully folded design is able to meet the requirements for

The Floquet process in twisted bilayer graphene at 2π flux creates a static momentum operator that is proportional to the integer 1 or -1. As a result, the momentum representation becomes controllable and conforms to conventional rules, enabling researchers to derive a wavefunction with a known momentum. Additionally, a static electric potential can be represented as a position operator, allowing the condition for the Landau levels to be determined. Observations reveal that the static electric field results in band splitting or merging, depending on the specific Landau level. Moreover, the static potential produces new mechanisms of chiral edge modes. Lastly, a proposed scheme involves using 2π flux to investigate topological properties, such as quantum anomalous Hall effects, which could be realized in twisted graphene samples by applying a gate voltage to modulate the momentum representation.

This research introduces a novel, hidden-compressed steering technique (HCS) that employs an LSTM-based model to create covert messages within text, leveraging the "twenty twentieth" linguistic phenomenon where identical sequences of characters frequently appear dispersively throughout English language texts. A model called iLST has been developed that identifies these instances, which have been scarce and hard to find manually. The proposed steering technique uses the identified sequences as "steering commands" to guide the LSTM to incorporate the secret message into the surrounding text. A comparative analysis was conducted, and the results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed HCS-iLST method over existing steganographic text approaches. Furthermore, it was successfully applied to two significant natural language inference tasks to enhance the robustness of the generated text against adversarial attacks.

Power unit commitment is a complex process that involves making decisions on which generating units to activate and offline within a specified time frame, taking into consideration constraints such as generation capacity, generator limitations, and spatial limitations, as well as maintenance requirements. This process can be formulated as an optimization problem with a large number of variables and constraints linked together over a long time period, often resulting in a vast solution space with complex relationships. In order to streamline the constraint checking process in unit commitment problems, researchers developed methods such as the "unfeasible region tracing" approach, tracing the areas where given constraints cannot be met, thus reducing computational time by bypassing these impractical solutions and fastening the unit commitment solution finding process.

Building on this concept, our study proposes an innovative method for constraint checking in unit commitment problems by leveraging the correlations between various constraints to optimize computational efficiency. By creating a parametrized model based on historical data and incorporating generator limitations, spatial limitations, and maintenance requirements, our approach enables the determination of feasible solutions in unit commitment problems by examining individual constraints in a streamlined process. In our experiments, our method outperformed other approaches by speeding up constraint checking by two times and reducing total computational time by five times.

Measurements using magnetic susceptibility and specific heat revealed that 
$\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ exhibits tunable magnetic properties under hydrostatic pressure. At ambient pressure, its magnetic Ir$^{4+}$ ions display a long-range spiral order that synchronizes with the crystal structure's symmetry. This spiral order persists until the pressure reaches around 14 kbar, at which point the magnetic properties start to change. This transition is accompanied by an abrupt drop in magnetic contribution to specific heat and susceptibility, signifying a possible emergence of nonmagnetic state under higher pressure. Moreover, an increase in pressure to 41 kbar causes the magnetic properties to completely disappear, while the nonmagnetic state reemerges upon further increasing the pressure. This behavior is attributed to structural changes caused by the increased pressure. To study this phenomenon, researchers used DFT calculations combined with a mean-field spin-heisenberg model. This theoretical model predicted that this change could result from the formation of dimers that disrupt the spiral order. Moreover, the structural changes caused by the pressure increase led to a shift of the X-ray diffraction peaks from (11$\overline{1}$) to (10$\overline{1}$) and ultimately to (111) directions. This result shows that the structural change of Ir$^{4+}$ dimers causes a shift of the XRD peaks.

This research develops a unifying theory for a synthesis-based approach to treating control groups, offering novel methodologies to address treatment effects on treated units as well as control groups. Treating the synthetic control for a treated subject alongside actual controls leads to new estimators with established asymptotic properties for within-subject treatment effects, comparisons of treated outcomes to controls, and treatment-specific baselines. These estimators include a t-statistic and confidence intervals for the latter, which we illustrate can be computed via easily accessible data summaries. Moreover, the theory accommodates a diverse range of pre-existing connections to machine learning, data imputation, and partial least squares, enabling the construction of universally valid inference intervals that do not demand specific covariance structures or dimensions. Synthetic control can be seen as a form of imputation, and our theory covers prominent applications such as principal components and partial least squares, which have been used widely.

This paper introduces a novel metric, known as Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, for capturing the differences in structural characteristics of distributed graph datasets. Building upon the established Gromov-Wasserstein framework, which effectively merges disparate graph structures while concealing node identity using random hashing, a pseudonymization technique is developed to ensure differential privacy for the graph key generation process. Furthermore, a modified random hash function, referred to as GW randomizer, is proposed to demonstrate the privacy preservation properties. Experimental evaluations of the proposed method demonstrate effective structural preservation using the Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy metric, in addition to validating the differential privacy properties.

Recent research has successfully injected relativistic electrons into dielectrics using highly intense laser pulses, achieving energies of a few hundred keV. However, the current understanding of this phenomenon remains incomplete due to the complex interaction between the electron plasma wave and the intense laser pulse, whose behavior changes qualitatively with increasing intensity. This qualitative shift, marked by the threshold intensity of approximately 19.6 erg/cm^2, is where the plasma wave's group velocity matches the laser pulse's velocity. Below this threshold, both electrons and plasma waves exhibit linear responses, whereas above it, the increased nonlinear interaction from higher intensity pulses accelerates electron injection. Consequently, this increased nonlinear interaction leads to more efficient electron injection and a unique 'polarization management' effect, where electrons are injected preferentially during the rising instead of the falling laser pulse phase. This experimentally demonstrated finding has been further validated through 3-dimensional particle-particle Monte Carlo simulations, suggesting a revised criterion for electron injection that reflects a more complex, high-intensity laser behavior.

The Platino experiment is a comprehensive study focused on understanding platinum isotopes and their potential interactions with dark matter, particularly in relationships. This ambitious project involves analyzing heavily shielded platinum detectors in a shallow underground location and has reported on the detection of over thirty thousand plastic-scintillator trips alongside platinum samples, as well as the investigation of isotopes and their potential links to background processes. As a result, the experiment has established new limits at specific quadrupole classes and has significantly improved existing limits for various types of nuclear transitions within platinum isotopes.

The calculation of the renormalization group scaling of the flavor-singlet axial-vector charge, responsible for quark charges non-uniformity, is performed in a comprehensive way, bridging a long-standing gap in understanding this process within the Standard Model when using the dimensional regularization method. Crucial to this calculation are the properties of operator product expansion, enabling the derivation of the operator that defines the charge, and a specific type of mathematical representation for the functional space of the QCD lagrangian, both essential for this purpose. Furthermore, this calculation accurately determines the properties of the anomaly, resolving inconsistencies from prior works, with implications that can validate the existence of a massless Baryon Asymmetry in Nature, albeit a very small one.

Driving comfort is greatly enhanced when the interior of a vehicle is not overly exposed to harsh outside light. Traditionally, drivers have relied on manual window tinting to achieve this, which blocks glare but also distorts the view of the road. We innovatively apply image tinting techniques, commonly used in image enhancement, to preserve the visual integrity of the driving scene while reducing its brightness. However, applying these methods to vehicle interiors poses significant challenges, primarily due to the absence of meaningful content - areas where the light should be admitted. Our proposed solution, called Cross-Camera Deep Tinting, overcomes these obstacles by decoupling window glass and scene areas, and using multiple camera inputs to combine undistorted window glass and scene images. We evaluate our method using two public datasets and demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches. Additional information and supplementary videos can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/cross-camera-tinting.

This study provides a comprehensive symmetries analysis along with conservation laws for the advanced and retarded generalized Ermakov systems in n dimensions. Constructing Lie algebras for the systems' point symmetries is also a key focus.

Predicting future demand for a transit network is a crucial task, as it can aid in allocating the necessary resources for new developments in an area. The Transit Feed Specification (TFS) is a standardized data format that records historical transit usage, but generating expected usage for unrecorded scenarios can be challenging due to limited data. A novel approach using Recurrent Neural Networks has been developed to forecast unobtainable TFS data, building upon existing methods that utilize Supervised Learning Networks. This new method utilizes Residual Recurrent Neural Networks, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to a conventional network on the Ottawa Valley Transportation Service data set. The source code for the proposed model has been made available on GitHub, providing users with the ability to customize it and achieve higher prediction accuracy.

Few-shot Prototyping Learning (FSL) aims to minimize the requirement of extensive labeled data in the learning process. The representation of prototypes plays a crucial role in the final model performance. Existing methods focus on representing individual samples, whereas this paper introduces an innovative approach where meta-class prototypes are developed for each group. We propose two flexible frameworks - the Condensed Prototype Framework and the Recurrent Prototype Framework - that can be utilized by a variety of models to design both intra-class and inter-class representations for meta-class prototypes by clustering a set of updated features. Our models incorporate a memory updater to eliminate unnecessary information and optimize computation, resulting in accurate feature representation through the minimization of distances between class means and sample features. Experimentation on multiple datasets reveals that our method achieves significant state-of-the-art results.

We're analyzing systems featuring persistent non-invertible symmetries, where these symmetries, despite not having an inverse, persist even in the presence of a perturbation. Non-invertible symmetries have a unique property where the composition of the symmetry's action on different parts of a state is zero. We've found that in systems with these persistent non-invertible symmetries, there is a fundamental connection to Goldstone modes, which often arise in this context. In particular, we've shown that the low-energy dynamics of these systems are constrained and can be determined by the symmetries' action on a specific state, resulting in a universal form that resembles a free fermion model. Notably, this effect is a direct result of the symmetries being both non-invertible and persistent, and it does not arise in systems with non-invertible symmeties that disappear with a perturbation or in systems with local symmetries. As an example of this phenomenon, we've shown that the low-energy behavior of a particular model of Majorana fermions in a specific environment exhibits this behavior, and it can also be applied to other similar scenarios.

A semi-transitive graph, with its edge relationships defined by paths of length at most two, has an edge transitivity of 1. Split graphs are comprised of a complete and bipartite subset, with high edge transitivity. The minimal split graph, containing all possible bipartite subsets, has an edge transitivity of either 1 or 3, depending on the subset. The following problems are being investigated: To what extent does the minimal split graph's high edge transitivity apply universally? Furthermore, can the universal splitting number be calculated using the maximum clique colouring number and other parameters?

A cutting-edge approach has been developed to pinpoint the distinctive characteristics of real tau particle decays in "tau-to-partons" events at the Large Hadron Collider. Past algorithms relied on a straightforward evaluation of observed particles and missing energy, but a deep neural network that analyzes these events as a whole has been trained to accurately identify genuine tau decays. This novel deep neural network has achieved an impressive classification accuracy of 82.2% -- significantly higher than previous methods -- when trained using the latest simulated data, distinguishing actual tau decays from those mimicked by other particles. Further analysis reveals that certain features, such as particle trajectories and total visible energy, play a crucial role in determining the probability of a tau decay, and future enhancements are planned to fine-tune this technique. This breakthrough will greatly aid physicists in understanding the behavior of Standard Model particles and will be a vital tool in analyzing exotic tau decays at the Large Hadron Collider.

We explore how to utilize Bayesian Neural Networks for classifying supernovae based on their light curves. Bayesian Neural Networks are a form of machine learning model that incorporate uncertainty into their design for probabilistic predictions. This makes them a promising candidate for supernovae research, particularly when dealing with rare events like type Ia supernovae. We investigate how to apply BNNs to the multi-band category system used by the Rubin Observatory's SN-EMTS project, as well as the SN-CNN model developed by SN-EMTS. Our experiments involve simulating supernovae curves using the TRES model and training BNNs to recognize rare patterns among these simulations. We achieve results that suggest BNNs can accurately label supernovae patterns as 'Rare' or 'Common' while providing probabilistic predictions, though BNNs struggle with the 'Normal' category. By merging the BNN model with the SN-CNN, we discover the merged model decreases classification accuracy in some instances. Our study also highlights the potential for leveraging Bayesian Neural Networks to take advantage of the density information from early-time rising sections of supernovae light curves.

Our study explores the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within solid-core photonic lattice fibers, comprising a fundamental mode and its first-order transverse mode. We demonstrate that the spatial structure of the fiber's photonic lattice core plays a significant role in the modal interaction through measurements of thermal optical nonlinearity and modal coupling coefficients. Notably, the measured values of these coefficients for 500 mm long photonic lattice fiber samples fall within the ranges of 0.38 - 0.91 cm^2/W and 0.38 - 0.76 cm^2/W, respectively, for the fundamental and transverse mode pairs. Moreover, the modal interaction enables tunable coupling between the fundamental and first-order modes via mechanical stress, thereby facilitating efficient energy transfer between the two modes.

For selected braided monoidal categories, excluding categories with non-trivial torsion, we establish a theorem stating that two functor mappings between categories of braided Coxeter groups are equivalent to a standard functor mapping if and only if these mappings share a common representation. Additionally, we prove that for Coxeter groups of type B, our theorem provides an equivalent statement to the foundational theorem of type A Coxeter groups.

Two problems, the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, can be solved using a combined approach. Initially, the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem is defined by a set of items, weights, and values, along with a budget and targets. The objective is to cover all indices with the given values while staying within the budget. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem is then described by non-negative weights and values across a set of subsets, aiming to maximize total values while staying within the budget by selecting a subset of subsets. A novel algorithm is introduced, using the solutions to the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem as candidates for the Subset Union Knapsack Problem, where candidates are combined based on their weights and values. The algorithm's efficiency is analyzed, showing a simple bound for its suboptimality, as well as an O(n log n + P) time complexity. Experimental results confirm the algorithm's effectiveness, combining the best of both problems and surpassing the individual solutions, where P represents problem size.

Churn prevention in business retention is a high-stakes issue, with numerous studies indicating extensive training data are necessary for achieving acceptable performance levels in this area. In contrast, our approach utilizes minimal user information to accurately predict churn in the online gaming sector, based on historical data. By analyzing 185, 357 player sessions from a real-world online casino, our models demonstrated impressive results, with a remarkable 75.6% precision in predicting churn and a modest 13.4% precision in ruling out churn. This effectiveness can be attributed to several crucial strategies employed by the casino operators.

We employ 2D lattice and spin models, combining the Ising and XY models, to study the Yang-Lee critical disorder tolerance. We start from the disorder-free Yang-Lee fixed point and apply it to the relevant RG flow, using it to determine the Yang-Lee fixed point's location within the 2D Ising model's field-space. We then derive a novel field-tuning representation of the 2D Ising model's Yang-Lee fixed point, focusing on the Yang-Lee edge and its intersection with the Fermi surface. This new representation allows us to distinguish between the Yang-Lee and Lee-Yang phases and to calculate the 2D Ising model's critical disorder tolerance. We also establish a novel field-theoretic description of the Yang-Lee fixed point, using complex scalar fields to represent the Yang-Lee edge's two real components. The Yang-Lee edge's propagation and self-interaction are derived using the Lee-Yang condition within the 2D Ising model's field theory. We then derive the critical disorder tolerance using the Yang-Lee edge's self-interaction and derive the Lee-Yang phase diagram, applying it to general 2D Ising field theories. We also study the effects of non-trivial critical disorder tolerances on the 2D Ising model's magnetic and thermal phase transitions and their critical exponents.

Our research demonstrates the ability to parton-distribute and parton-factorize
complex complex-valued functions that depend on the virtuality, aligning with
the principles of large-momentum effective theory. We introduce two key functions,
the gluon ball function, $H_b(z)$ and the gluon ball bullet function,
$H_1(z)$, and provide explicit expressions for their scale-dependent evolution.
Our findings show that the gluon distribution $g(z)$ and the gluon kernel $C_{g},
$ remain unchanged even at extremely large virtualities, thus rendering the
virtuality-independent the gluon TMD, $A_{T}\{g,\xi\}$. This has significant
consequences, as it enables the calculation of $\bar g \otimes \bar g$ to
first-order TMD calculations and allows the derivation of the unpolarized
TMD gluon distribution, $A_{T}\{g,\xi\}$. Additionally, our research reveals
that the gluon TMD, $A_{T}\{g,\xi\}$, is insensitive to the effects of
Asymmetrical Strong Hypercolor Interaction and that the $\xi$-dependent, non-
perturbative su(3)Y model of gluon TMD distribution can be represented by a single
free parameter, $\xi_0$.

In the photon-photon interactions that occur during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through processes such as vector meson decay and the vector dominance effect. These electron-positron pairs can then interact with the large nuclear charge of the colliding ions via a range of electromagnetic forces. A comprehensive analysis is presented in this work, focusing on the emission of electron- and positron pairs in the interaction with large nuclei: considering initial low-momentum electron- and positron states, the analysis includes coherent photon interaction, inelastic processes such as Compton scattering and Bhabha scattering, as well as the possibility of vector meson decay. The findings of this work indicate that while vector meson decay dominates the production of electron- and positron pairs at low momentum, the photonuclear interactions are significantly suppressed. Furthermore, the analysis shows that the photonuclear interactions are predominantly inelastic, except for particles with very low momentum. The study shows that by examining the momentum distribution of the produced electron- and positron pairs, it is possible to gain insights into the spatial distribution of the photons within the colliding ions, as well as their electric fields. A range of possible experimental signatures that could allow the confirmation of the predicted effects is also discussed in this work.

To minimize the severity of injuries resulting from bike accidents, a reliable method for forecasting near-crash events is needed. This study presents an innovative solution called RiskMAP, a real-time system that uses computer vision to identify situations for cyclists, drivers, and other road users. By analyzing broadcast soccer games, the researchers have developed an effective approach for detecting near-crash events from broadcast video footage. By combining map data with the detected events, the system generates a heat map display that indicates the level of risk along a road route. This display, referred to as a Risk Map, provides a visual representation of the road user's journey, highlighting the areas where incidents have been detected. The study's results show that the RiskMAP model achieved high accuracy when classifying bike, motorbike, and car trajectories, with an F1 score of 0.96. The resulting prototype has been successfully tested by road users, yielding positive feedback. The researchers believe that this technology will contribute significantly to reducing the risk of road accidents by pinpointing high-risk locations and prompting preventive measures before accidents occur.

The practical implementation of any robotics system in real-world environments is challenged by uncertainty stemming from dynamic processes and incomplete knowledge of the surrounding environment. Existing robotics systems that utilize Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) often fail to address these issues effectively as they rely on inaccurate estimates of the state and assume known dynamic parameters, or require complex online optimization processes. To overcome these limitations, a novel Motion Planning approach is introduced, based on a new type of CBF that can be easily integrated with a wide array of pre-existing motion planning algorithms and trajectories to achieve superior robustness and security. This method enables the computation of a safe and robust trajectory given uncertain dynamics and initial conditions by leveraging a new type of CBF known as the Power-CBF. Different from traditional CBFs that can only provide safety guarantees for a limited period of time, the Power-CBF allows for both safety and robustness to be guaranteed for an indefinite amount of time, as it can be repeatedly used to obtain new, safer trajectories until the desired goal is reached. This method can be efficiently used with a variety of motion planning algorithms through a process of iterative inverse optimization, or within a feedback planning framework for even greater efficiency. This approach is verified through its successful application to a mobile robot navigating around obstacles both in simulation and in a real-world test and also to a quadrotor in simulation.

For a finite ring R with n elements, this paper defines 'enveloping numbers' n_v such that any subset V of R satisfies n_v if and only if the subset is a generating set. It provides the exact values of n_v for rings with 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 elements and establishes methods for calculating n_v for subsets of size 2, whereas the cases involving larger subset sizes remain unresolved.

Deep neural networks are highly vulnerable to manipulations by a limited category of data, which includes techniques such as adversarial examples and image manipulations. The fact that they frequently output predictions that don't match the actual data labels, raising concerns about trustworthiness in critical applications such as medical imaging. Researchers have developed various methods to counteract the susceptibility of DNNs to adversarial examples. The objective of this research is to explore strategies for enhancing robustness in line with the idea of natural resilience, which focuses on performing well on genuine data that reflects the patterns in the real world. In this research, we examine the state of the art in adversarial attacks and defenses, with an emphasis on understanding the connections between natural image distribution and adversarial attacks. Additionally, we investigate certain natural defense methods: natural data preprocessing, excluding training data subsets, and natural adversarial attacks that draw on statistical characteristics of natural image distributions.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions of the form $b(\xi(x,t),\eta(x,t))$, where $\xi$ and $\eta$ represent spatial and temporal local averages of a solution and its spatial derivative, respectively, are the subject of investigation. These nonlocal equations encompass a broad range of applications, including traditional scalar conservation laws and multidimensional traffic models. We establish a singular limit result, demonstrating that any admissible, locally Lipschitz entropy-solution of the nonlocal PDEs arises as the limit, under appropriate norm convergences, of a corresponding local PDE. Furthermore, applying the Oleinik-Kopp-Morawetz entropy condition leads to an evaluation of the convergence rate. Crucially, this rate depends only on the Lipschitz constant of the flux function and is independent of its nonlocal aspects. As a consequence, it follows that any entropy-solution of the nonlocal PDEs, which is also locally Lipschitz in space and time, is in the singular limit (as the nonlocal parameter vanishes) an entropy-solution of the corresponding local PDE.

Dilation surfaces are a type of smooth surface equipped with a hyperbolic metric that expands at a constant rate within a contractive framework. Dilation surfaces feature distinctive characteristics such as constant scalar curvature and a dual graph comprising tree structures. A key aspect of this study involves classifying the singularities present on dilation surfaces using their indices, leading to the concept of index dual graphs. By examining the generic configuration of dilation surfaces, researchers identify a particular class of singularities known as dilation singularities, which possess an indefinite metric component and a specific configuration in the dual graph. A key finding reveals that all dilation surfaces feature a universal type of singular link known as the horizon saddle link. Moreover, studies demonstrate that a dilation surface exhibits smooth behavior when the indices of its singularities meet specific criteria, prompting researchers to define a particular structure, known as a dilation structure. Results show that a dilation surface possesses this structure when it satisfies certain conditions and, further, that a dilation surface exhibits Morse-Smale behavior when its dual graph comprises tree structures, leading to the definition of a particular class of dilation surfaces known as minimal. Studies reveal that all minimal dilation surfaces possess smooth structures, demonstrating that a particular type of horizon saddle link is singular and non-contractible, and finally, indicating that a specific type of dilation surface known as generalized Martin surface is, in fact, a non-generic dilation surface.

Recent studies suggest certain brain disorders are linked to distorted functional connections. However, identifying and understanding these changes presents a significant challenge due to the high complexity and noisy data of functional brain networks. We propose an efficient method to evaluate the relationships between different brain regions by utilizing total correlation, which can be calculated efficiently with Monte Carlo simulations. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by revealing distinct patterns of correlation in both healthy and abnormal brains, such as during altered states of consciousness and Alzheimer's disease. This method has the advantage of being adaptable to various applications of functional brain analysis.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms linked to the Schrödinger operator, highlighting their interconnection 
as a consequence of the Taylor isomorphism. This study generalizes those concepts 
to operators provided by Clifford algebra, a type of first-order matrix operator, 
thus extending existing work from Albert and Ballester-Belles. It looks at three 
unitary isomorphisms related to Clifford algebra operators, focusing on the limit 
operator and its link to the min-max theory through the square root of such an 
operator. The work includes a detailed look at the weighted Bergman space connected 
to the Clifford algebra, along with its weighted multi-variable monomials.

In the context of Gaussian fields, we propose a novel form of field-to-field conditioning distinct from the traditional second-order conditioning based on the field's values and its derivatives. Our field-to-field conditioning utilizes the field's local extremes and its logarithmic increments. We demonstrate that a Gaussian field is conditionally Gaussian given its extreme values and its locally computed increments. Furthermore, we leverage this new conditioning technique to design innovative tests for uniform deviation and extreme value occurrences, and we establish optimal sample size criteria for these tests through the calculation of a characteristic logarithmic extremum variance. We also examine how these new tests compare with their value-only counterparts.

This study examines the creation of a integrated sensing and communication system that utilizes a single radio interface. The objective is to develop a scalable, distributed algorithm that selects and coordinates communication within the ground-and-air sensor network through the use of drones. The proposed solution involves utilizing a subgradient-based approach to solve a semi-definite programming (SDP) optimization problem that ensures a stable and interconnected network while allowing each node to interact directly with its most distant neighbors. By developing this interpersonal connectivity, aerial nodes are able to communicate with ground-based sensors while achieving full network connectivity. Additionally, the effectiveness of our proposed link establishment method is demonstrated through simulation results presented in gamma-ray radiation scenarios.

The discovery of neutrino oscillations established not one but multiple flavors of neutrinos. Research on neutrinos has expanded our understanding of their role in physics, particularly their role in the universe's lepton symmetry. By investigating neutrino properties with increasingly precise measurements, scientists aim to gain insight into fundamental particle physics. A major project, the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), is at the forefront of this research, designed to detect neutrino interactions at a remote location deep within a mountain. DUNE's first-stage development is currently underway with the aim of commencing data collection in 2027. DUNE's first-phase will utilize a 1-10 GeV energy range neutrino detector, located 1 km from a massive target made of high-quality plastic, virgin to human contact. DUNE first-phase is well-positioned to meet DUNE's objectives which include: the precise measurement of neutrino properties, a comprehensive study of electron neutrino appearance in muon neutrino interactions with the ultimate goal of establishing the order parameter. Additionally, DUNE aims to meet its goals of conducting accurate measurements in its path to precision, meeting particle physics research objectives and contributing to global neutrino research.

A crucial task in high-energy physics is top identification. Top tagging involves finding more than one top quark in an event, which is significant in discovering new heavy particles that decompose into top quarks. Prior studies have shown top tagging methods utilizing linear models. However, linear models are insufficient for capturing the complexity of the top tagging problem's interactions. We developed an improved top tagging method utilizing gradient boosted trees, which surpasses previous tags in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, our study introduces a novel technique to analyze the contributions of individual input features in a complex predictive model, despite them being complex and interdependent. This method, inspired by cooperative game theory, allows for a deeper understanding of the relationships between input features and the classifier's decisions. We discovered that specific physics events, such as t-tbar and heavy particles decaying into top quarks, can be distinguished based on the collective importance of a small group of input features.

This document offers a comprehensive mathematical representation of Virtual Organizations and their advancement. It serves as a foundation for validating the virtual organization manager's decisions regarding resource allocation, as well as providing a starting point for verifying the manager's correctness through formal mathematical proofs.

Efficient policy optimization in complex, high-dimensional games like Atari necessitates comprehensive experience replay across various levels of the game's hierarchy. Although conventional replay techniques work well with value-based algorithms, their effectiveness heavily depends on the specific algorithm being used. This research presents a novel approach to experience replay that facilitates efficient optimization by reducing the variance of policy evaluation, thus enabling faster convergence and improved performance in a broader range of scenarios. To achieve this, we establish a connection between the generalized advantage estimation method and functional PCA, then design a new sampling technique that efficiently utilizes this association to vary reducing the expectation of value targets. Our proposed approach outperforms existing methods, leading to better performance and faster convergence in a range of challenging games.

Two new strategies, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization, have been proposed to deal with the antisymmetric density matrix within an antinormally ordered context, resulting from the application of functional integration. Both methods yield the same outcome when applied to a path integral, each yielding a specific expression involving the density matrix and its relationship to Gaussian integrals. However, when used to derive the effective action from a path-integral formula, different results emerge, indicating a dependence on the third moment of the quasiparticle spectrum. Notably, the effective action derived from the superbosonization method reveals an invariance to the quasiparticle spectrum, unlike the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. The derivation of the effective action from a Hermitian two-body operator is provided as an example demonstration.

In various tasks such as vehicle design refinement and disease therapy optimization, developing detailed and accurate motion models is essential. However, existing models like physics-based data-driven methods and deep learning auto-regressive techniques have limitations, especially in large-scale applications and real-world environments. A proposed solution, Motion Aspects Learning, utilizes spatiotemporal sequences to identify and learn key motion characteristics, offering improved interpretability and flexibility in both long-term and online prediction applications. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, a simple and efficient RNN-based method, MoDeRNN, is introduced with experiments performed on a vehicle dynamics dataset. The proposed method achieves high-quality motion understanding and prediction, while also showcasing refined motion aspects through feature visualization and analysis.

This research focuses on achieving memory safety in object-oriented programming languages by incorporating concepts from type theory, but deviates from existing approaches by also addressing the problem of safely handling asynchronous programs. A key challenge in this area stems from the inherent race conditions present in programs that utilize shared memory concurrently. This issue is particularly evident in Rust's concept of ownership and borrowing, which is compromised when asynchronous tasks are involved, ultimately leading to a variety of memory-related errors. This paper aims to demonstrate how the principles of universal coinductivity can be applied to asynchronized programs in a shared-memory setting. Furthermore, it proposes a novel programming model that leverages the benefits of asynchronous programming via coroutines, while also ensuring memory safety by incorporating the following key aspects: memory safety, universal coinductivity, pure state effects, and control effects. However, achieving memory safety in this model proves to be a complex task, requiring the use of effect types to incorporate asynchronous tasks. This paper introduces an innovative typing discipline that synchronizes asynchronous tasks with other memory-related tasks. A key aspect of this discipline is its ability to avoid the limitations of flow-sensitive typing, which is essential for ensuring memory safety in this setting. This typing discipline is further expanded by incorporating the principles of effect-envelopes, which are essential for precisely identifying the effects present in programs. A key advantage of this discipline is its ability to incorporate a variety of programming paradigms, including asynchronous programming, object-oriented programming, functional programming, and imperative programming

Studies on neutrinoless double-beta decay from colliders offer unique insights into how Majorana neutrinos interact. The research focuses on the interactions between two identical neutrinos and a heavy particle with a large mass, where the decay modes are influenced by both the particle's spin and whether it decays evenly. Calculations, conducted across a wide range of energies, explore the interplay between Majorana states in this context, with findings applied to a specific collider: the Future Circular Collider. The research provides a comprehensive analysis of this decay, including the interplay between these particles, in colliders.

Permutation decoding is a highly efficient solution for decoding linear codes under random perturbation. We developed a novel approach by integrating belief propagation decoding and a polar subcode, allowing us to scale this efficiency up for higher-rate polar codes. We derived a subcode decomposition formula and suggested a practical method to enumerate common subvectors between the polar code and the original code, which can then be combined into a parallel subcode through convolution, both of which contribute to the final decoding outcome. This proposed scheme is accompanied by simulations that demonstrate its performance.

Images captured by space telescopes often get distorted by a phenomenon called trailing off at the edges. To improve the clarity of these images, astronomers combine multiple captured images, despite this combination often resulting in irregular image shapes. To better understand the composition of celestial bodies, astronomers need a more in-depth understanding of how colors and light behave in these combined images. To tackle this, we developed a mathematical approach for a specific type of irregular image shape, and then applied it to determine the effective point of focus for combined images. We explored different techniques to extract this information, analyzing which one provides the most accurate results. To validate our findings, we analyzed combined images of the galaxy M51 using a specific technique that adjusts image clarity, and discovered notable differences between the galaxy's center and surrounding areas.

The fracture strength of fourteen solid materials, ranging from minerals to engineering metals and alloys, all with well-documented atomic structures, is examined using the type of theoretical method employed in our earlier study [G. S. Pawar, S. P. S. Sidhu, S. P. S. The type of theoretical method employed in our earlier study[G. S.  G.  G.  Pawar, S.  S.  S.  Sidhu, S.  P.  P.  S.  S.  S.  from  Pawar et al 2016]. We found that by setting the fracture strength to approximately 10 times the material's density, we were able to predict the material's fracture strength with great accuracy. This was shown in our work, where the average discrepancy between predicted and actual fracture strengths was around 24 percent. This study shows that understanding how many electrons are in a material's 3d orbitals is very important in determining a material's fracture strength. Materials with fewer 3d electrons tend to have higher fracture strengths, and those with fewer 3d electrons tend to have lower elastic properties. Additionally, this study shows that materials with a mix of 3d and 4s, 4p, and 4d, 4i electrons tend to have lower fracture strengths. Quantum field theories model complex phenomena in physics, chemistry, and biology. However, the underlying tools to analyze these theories are often simplistic compared to the sophisticated methods used in probability theory and mathematical physics. This article explores the connection between these two worlds, specifically by using multiple SLEs driven by chaotic electrons to better understand conformal field theory. We use specific formulas, called trace formulas, to understand this connection. These formulas include a correlation function formula that explains how conformal field theories work, and a spectral formula that explains how conformal field theories are related to each other. We use these formulas to prove a relationship between the Gaussian free field and multiple SLEs, and in doing so we simplify the path that experts Gershgorin and Scheie previously took.
For the 3D periodic Navier-Stokes equations, estimates of the solution's maximum amplitude are obtained relative to the initial conditions.

The growing presence of quantum computing raises significant concerns about ensuring the accuracy and security of quantum-aided systems. 
This security reliance hinges heavily on an efficient and traditional verification method that checks quantum computations for accuracy.
Research has devised several verification approaches, such as probabilistic checking and algorithms like the Brahymer-Hayden routine, 
which verifies quantum information through classical simulation but operates in quadratic time, thereby limiting its scope due to cost constraints.
This study addresses this limitation by developing and successfully testing a traditional verification algorithm that works in linear time.
