A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Aquila-Xe complex was created by combining the observations from Gaia DR2 and GALEX's far-ultraviolet spectrum scans. The analysis revealed that dust in the Taurus complex absorbs starlight at specific wavelengths, causing the observed far-ultraviolet spectrum variations. By comparing our data with models that simulate the effects of dust absorption, we adjusted the dust parameters and also used the data to measure the total dust mass in the region, which we found to be approximately 5500-6800 solar masses. Furthermore, an increased amount of gas and dust in the region was detected using LASS-J1604-211, a nearby young stellar object with a strong far-ultraviolet spectrum emissions, and we determined this increased material amounts to approximately 33-100 solar masses and 110-310 solar masses respectively for gas and dust. Lastly, by further studying the variation in total extinction as it relates to distance across the region and using observations of both unclustered stars and the increased material amounts, we confirmed that the increased material amounts are increased uniformly across the region and the region's structure conforms to the predicted two-dimensional model of a star-forming region.

Document search techniques in digital libraries are now capable of searching not just text-based information, but also entire documents including tables. However, current table search methods are limited in their ability to retrieve a table when given a description, even when descriptions are written by humans. This is due in part to the various formats in which tables may be saved - image, XML, HTML - which can affect the success of a query. To improve table retrieval from descriptions, a model employing graph neural networks successfully extracts table representations from different formats, enabling a generic table query. Experiments using a small set of human-written descriptions achieved impressive results, demonstrating the validity of this approach. Further experiments revealed that the model's success may depend on the quality of the embeddings used to represent the description and the table. While tables with simple descriptions tend to be correctly identified, adding description quality as an input variable does not entirely explain the model's behavior in cases of incorrect table retrieval.

This study investigates the high cognitive demands of multi-step decision-taking games where players have limited information. Building on the initial findings of Banach and Smaglik [2020], this research classifies cognitive levels in incomplete information games, starting from the simple concept of a single-stage game with no information, progressing through imperfectly informed two-stage games to perfectly informed two-stage games, and finally considering three-stage games with perfect information. To facilitate this classification, this work makes two key contributions: firstly, it develops a unique method for analyzing three-stage games with perfect information by representing them as a pair of two-stage games, and secondly, it employs simplified models of incomplete information two-stage games, such as the Franz-Parro-Pombo game and the one-shot game. Using these tools, this research identifies distinct levels of cognitive sophistication in incomplete information games, showcases cognitive advancements in specific game transformations, and provides a thorough characterization of the first two levels of cognitive sophistication in both single-stage and two-stage games with imperfect information. Building on the initial findings of Banach and Smaglik [2020], this study culminates with a complete classification of the three levels of cognitive sophistication in incomplete information games.

The COVID-19 pandemic revealed weaknesses in population estimation systems, as seen in the excessive delays and inaccuracies experienced in censuses. To prevent such vulnerabilities, enhanced strategic planning for censuses is essential, especially in regards to using remote sensing technology. A potential solution is the development of a fully autonomous population estimation system, and in this paper, we explore the potential of such a system, examining the data requirements and a proposed approach for the development of an affordable, accurate, and robust system suitable for the demographics of Mozambique. We also investigate the effect of various factors on the accuracy of population prediction models, providing an understanding of the constraints of such a system and highlighting potential applications. Our research aims to contribute to the development of a fully autonomous population estimation system, a crucial step in the evolution of population estimation.

In practical scenarios, high rates of false positives due to inaccurate approximations can render AMQFs less effective for real-time data analysis. While several innovative algorithms have been proposed to minimize errors, their use remains limited due to the inability to guarantee the absence of false positives. To overcome this challenge, we present an original solution called the Single-Purpose Approximate Table (SPAN) that ensures zero false positives while maintaining acceptable query times. SPAN employs a structured collection format, merges entries along query axes, and employs an optimized ordering to minimize query processing time. Experimental results using both synthesized and public data demonstrate that SPAN achieves negligible query times with only a modest storage precost. For example, storing 10% more data enables query times under 10 milliseconds using a system with a 1 GB storage capacity. Compared to existing AMQF approaches, SPAN accelerates query processing by 1-3 orders of magnitude.

We theoretically investigated the process of three-body recombination in a two-electron atomic system under a short-pulse laser, which leads to the creation of molecules in a superposition of states. This study reveals that, by adjusting the laser parameters, the resulting molecular wave function can be optimized to meet specific requirements. Our analysis shows that, apart from optimizing coherence between states of the same symmetry as the initial state, a specific phase of the wave function also plays a crucial role in this process, which could be achieved by adjusting the polarization of the laser pulse. This finding can be further utilized in experiments to study the properties of spin-orbit interactions in bosonic atoms. Additionally, we have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach using an example based on the manipulation of spin and orbital angular momentum in nd-series atoms.

Over the past twenty years, SPH has primarily been used in scientific research to model the interactions of water and solid objects, with numerous applications in fields such as engineering and physics. Yet, despite its success, SPH has several limitations, particularly when it comes to accurately representing the composition of multi-component systems, where different materials coexist. To address this challenge, a multi-resolution SPH framework is developed, with a groundbreaking approach that exploits the dual nature of SPH to tackle the problem. By incorporating both extensions of SPH, the framework achieves a high degree of accuracy and stability in modeling multi-component fluid-structure interactions, as demonstrated in the paper's closing section through two exemplary case studies. These examples showcase the framework's capabilities in handling fluid-structure interactions with multi-component materials, as well as its ability to handle multi-component flows interacting with rigid objects.

We utilize a superconducting quantum processor with 40 qubits to explore
unsupervised machine learning methods, specifically applying them to two
datasets: binary patterns of decreasing similarity and a sequence of
connected values. For the first task, an algorithm is designed to
automatically group similar instances by converting the problem into a
minimum-cut problem and applying a quantum algorithm to find an optimal
cut. For the second, a recursive process is employed to gradually construct
a dynamic model from the current and past states. When compared to classical
methods, our results demonstrate that the quantum processor can either
accomplish tasks faster or produce equivalent results with lower energy
requirements. These experiments mark the first application of unsupervised
learning techniques to quantum systems.

Research into speech synthesis via neural networks has recently made significant strides, driven by demands for more controllable and high-fidelity speech models. The FastPitch model, a time-series cross-attention-based model, excels at speech synthesis and provides fine-grained pitch control using a duration-conditioned model. Nonetheless, achieving even the smallest changes in pitch often results in considerable changes to the speaker's vocal characteristics. This paper proposes an advanced method for adjusting pitch, known as timbre-preservation pitch augmentation (TPPA), which can refine the pitch control even further. The proposed TPPA method trains a neural transformation module to transform pitch features based on a limited vocabulary of melodic notes, enabling more precise control over pitch changes while maintaining the need for additional processing. The effectiveness of the TPPA method was evaluated through various experiments, which demonstrated improved speech quality and pitch control.

This study targets spatiotemporal modeling, where we design a multi-hop
inference network, named Hopper, for predicting 3D objects' positions in autonomous driving scenarios.
Hopper employs a transformer-based model that predicts object states in sequence using features from convolutional networks.
The novel aspect of our work involves developing a multi-hop inference framework for aggregating features and encoding spatiotemporal relationships among objects.
We also introduce a dynamic graph for modeling attention between objects, leading to superior multi-hop inference performance.
Hopper's sparsity and dynamic graph design facilitate faster inference and improved computational efficiency.
Experimental results demonstrate that our Hopper achieves state-of-the-art performance while using a significantly reduced number of parameters, showing up to 71\% parameter reduction relative to the top-performing model, with only a limited loss in accuracy (0.3 points).

This research paper presents theoretical findings on the production of $W$ bosons in conjunction with a pair of $W$ bosons or Higgs bosons, accompanied by two leptons. We examine production at the Large Hadron Collider using next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamics, focusing on the actual $W$ mass determination. Our calculations include the intricate effects of final $b\bar{b}$ pairs that hampers accurate measurements of the $W$ boson mass. We find that despite the decreased contribution of this background compared to similar processes with only $W$ bosons, it still has a minor impact on precision $W$ mass measurements of around 0.03 GeV. We provide concrete examples of this in the specific context of the Single Electron Topical Group's proposed measurement.

Remote-controlled telepresence robots have seen growing popularity in recent years due to their versatility in both personal and professional applications, thanks to advancements in technology. A key factor contributing to their appeal is the immersive user experience they offer, which enables individuals to connect remotely with others in person and vice versa. In this context, it is crucial to understand how users respond to the performance of these systems, especially when navigating robotic platforms interactively. To address this need, we developed and tested a new method for measuring Quality of Experience (QoE) that utilizes a drive simulator to replicate the effects of network delays and speeds on remote navigation through a telepresence robot. A user study involving 36 participants evaluated the simulator with different time parameters and revealed significant variations in user satisfaction levels despite similar navigation distances. Our research marks an important step in the QoE area, providing a practical example of how to engage users in quality-assessment processes.

In educational measurement, various real-world data exhibit complexity, such as non-normality, heteroscedasticity, and underlying group structures, as opposed to the classical uniform distribution. A suitable method of analyzing such data is a Bayesian hierarchical linear model, which helps make informed decisions by providing precise context measurements. This study introduces a simple overview of these models, specifically focusing on their applications in various educational settings, such as assessing learning effectiveness across multiple subjects and understanding teacher biases using Bayesian hierarchical models. It is worth noting that decision-making situations in educational settings involve moderate to high-stakes consequences, although the presented models are generally versatile and applicable to many fields outside educational measurement. The paper includes an extensive example of using the models, utilizing artificially created data with non-uniform distributions, as well as presenting the results of applying the models using Python code for reproduction.

The game of Mafia involves players taking on specific roles with distinct abilities, including the mysterious role of Mafia. A comprehensive mathematical model for this game has been established to analyze strategies. This paper presents a detailed description of this framework, outlining both independent and collaborative games, as well as discussing potential applications and strategies within this theoretical framework.

This study examines the coexistence of gas giants during the accretion phase, exploring how their mutual relationship affects their final mass and the surrounding protoplanetary disk's composition. A model of interacting gas giants is developed and integrated into a viscous, turbulent disk where the surface density changes over time and distance. A key feature of this model is the gas giant model's ability to efficiently accumulate mass by drawing in surrounding gas, particularly at low orbital periods. As gas giants mature, their capture of gas decreases, and their growth slows, with a maximum accretion efficiency seen when their orbital periods are between 5-20 years. If gas giants remain isolated, they reach an optimal mass, but concurrent interaction with a companion can reduce this mass by up to 20% due to gas transfer, which occurs when the companion's orbital period falls within the 5-20 year range. Furthermore, when gas giants interact with a dense disk, they can redirect gas towards their companion, potentially increasing the companion's mass by as much as 50%. As a result, interactions between gas giants in dense disks can lead to the simultaneous presence of low-mass planets and high-mass giants. A possible consequence of this phenomenon is the creation of planetary systems featuring numerous low-mass planets in highly crowded orbital configurations around massive gas giants.

The electrical conductivity of a single-wall carbon nanotubes, when applied in a thin film, can be difficult to understand due to the complex interaction between the nanotubes. By examining the conductivity of an armchair nanotube film at low temperature and varying levels of light exposure, our findings reveal the importance of light on the electrical properties of these materials. Moreover, our results show that as the light exposure increases, the films' behavior shifts from a semiconducting to a metallic state. Through the analysis of a two-carrier model that includes both electrons and photons, it became clear that the change in behavior was due to the increased photoexcitation of electrons. What is more surprising is that as the exposure continued to increase, the films' conductivity began to decrease. This phenomenon was found to be caused by the increased phonon activity which suppressed the intertube electronic conduction. Ultimately, the results demonstrate the significance of both photophysics and photophony in determining the intertube electronic conduction of these materials.

This research develops a novel entropy-driven variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data with minimal information available for each feature. A proposed entropy-evaluation criterion is utilized to select relevant features and assess their contribution to clustering performance. Meanwhile, a variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means algorithm clusters data with the assistance of multiple relevant features while giving different weights to each one based on their individual contributions. Numerical computations, accompanied by several three-dimensional datasets and a real-world 120-dimensional stock dataset, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach.

The Mixture-of-Experts model has been a cornerstone for generative modeling and ensemble learning, but conventional optimization techniques frequently yield poorly trained ensemble structures, hindering the model's potential. To overcome this challenge, we develop a straightforward yet effective optimization method that incorporates an advanced form of weight normalization and a unified feed-forward decomposition for MoE models. By doing so, we derive an interesting connection to the Principal Axis Regression technique. The results of our method are then compared against state-of-the-art techniques in both supervised and unsupervised learning contexts, showcasing the method's capability to yield superior quality models with enhanced computational efficiency.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, focusing on classes of primitive primitive Jacobians and Pryms defined by the chip-firing game. It also outlines the criteria for determining the isomorphic groups based on chip-firing games.

Despite decades of research into quantum gravity, its fundamental nature remains unclear, largely due to a lack of concrete experimental guidance. We present an experimental approach proposing that quantum gravity may reveal itself through the global symmetry that governs nature on both the large-scale cosmic and laboratory terahertz wave lengths. A recent study of non-linear electric field propagation in nature has provided fresh evidence of a previously unaccounted interaction affecting double refraction. We demonstrate how existing measurements of double refraction can be reinterpreted to set a lower bound on the scale at which global symmetries break, estimated to be approximately 10^66 GeV, a value that surpasses current theoretical expectations of Planck vibrations. If this expectation holds, it could pave the way for a breakthrough in understanding quantum gravity by facilitating a new generation of experiments designed to detect and study the phenomenon of electric-matter coupling in nature on the Planck scale.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters. These findings were obtained through ultraviolet ITT/Grasp observations conducted from 17 December 2016 to 31 December 2016. In partnership with prior studies in the Strömgren photometric system, our analysis aimed to identify post-main sequence stars on the horizontal branch by analyzing FUV to optical color combinations. Moreover, our investigation also aimed to examine the effects of binary contamination on the distributions of FUV-colour distributions. Furthermore, our analysis aimed to examine the statistical associations between FUV colours and horizontal branch star features, specifically X-ray and variability. Last, our analysis aimed to examine the relationships between FUV colours and the characteristics of white dwarf stars, specifically temperature and luminosity.

The underlying concept of the b-principle revolves around the idea of separating a complicated function into two more manageable parts, where one of them is straightforward to evaluate while the space associated with the other function is relatively flexible in nature. The core principle lies in the fundamental notion that flexible spaces can give rise to flexible measures, which in turn enables the derivation of various flexibility results across various fields of mathematics. The primary objective of this article is to outline a strategy for demonstrating the fragile variant of the b-principle by using the Cohen-Mumford rigidity theorem as a key example.

This paper undertakes a thorough examination of the transfer learning, identifying two fundamental guarantees, or agreements, that are thought to contribute to its success. The first agreement concerns the relationship between a model's training and its target prediction, or loss, and its performance after adaptation. The second agreement, or assumption, relates to the similarity between two distributions, implying that a model optimized for one distribution can be effectively applied to another, or 'close enough'. We argue that these two agreements are spurious, or unnecessary, and instead propose a new theory based on the idea that a model optimized for one task can incorporate another task in a new one, or 'extend upon', effectively improving overall results.

In various scenarios, such as marketing and contagion, the swift spread of information and phenomena can yield more substantial outcomes. The accelerated dissemination has been attributed to numerous factors, including the critical mass of agents reaching a consensus and the peak of infectiousness reaching a peak value. By simulating the dynamics of a susceptible-infected model on artificial networks whose structure is a random gas-like arrangement, we have found that the speed of information spread is faster in networks where a community structure is present. Furthermore, our results show that the efficiency of information dissemination increases with the level of network modularity, indicating that a well-organized network infrastructure can enhance the efficiency of information spread.

We establish a novel quantitative measure of distinctiveness for closed, gaussian-free J-holomorphic curves in C^2, which refinements of the Thom-Yau distinctiveness criterion. The established criterion has significant implications in various areas of study, particularly in the estimation of counting outcomes from singular, non-absolute J-holomorphic curve integrals, such as those related to tri-constellations and disk-to-cylinder boundaries.

We propose a new approach for analyzing the regular perturbation model in discrete-time channels by leveraging concepts from stochastic approximation. This framework allows us to derive explicit conditions and criteria for ensuring the asymptotic stability of the channel state trajectory, which can be used to develop accurate prediction tools for regular perturbation models. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to two specific scenarios - Gaussian and log-concave channels - and establish explicit termination criteria for simulated recurrences, which confirm our theoretical findings and validate the asymptotic stability of the channel state trajectory.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. This type of malware can be found in all stages of its life cycle, from entry-level malware to sophisticated malware that adapts to new environments. Android's features, such as app sandboxing and dynamic permission grants, make it easy for malware to evade detection by bypassing security measures like permission verification. As a result, attackers seek to bypass these security features by achieving success in subsequent stages of the evasion attack process, specifically evading detection beyond installed app spaces by achieving system space evasion. This document explores a study on evasion attacks against Android, with a particular focus on a sub-category called issue-space evasion attacks, which necessitate altering app behaviors by manipulating issues, such as app crashes, to achieve this goal. The study discusses the varied nature of evasion attacks against Android, with a focus on this sub-category, with the aim of assisting developers and security professionals in protecting Android users from these types of attacks.

This paper introduces Ozy, a novel container designed to efficiently manage and coordinate the execution of workloads with varied architectures. Unlike traditional container systems, Ozy boasts a portable and flexible design that seamlessly adapts to executing either cloud-native or traditional workloads. Furthermore, Ozy ensures a streamlined and efficient execution environment by leveraging fine-grained isolation mechanisms, thereby ensuring minimal overhead while providing near-native performance. Our innovative container features an adaptable runtime with dynamic memory management, transparent security via isolation, and dynamic networking capabilities. Ozy's proof-of-concept includes a lightweight and compact executor, sample apps from both old and new architectures, along with a demonstration of its features through a demonstration experiment that showcases its performance, efficiency, and functionality.

In our study, we investigate the effect of Landau levels mixing on particle-hole symmetry in a 5-dimensional quantum Hall system, characterized by a specific finiteness gap in the spectrum. Utilizing SU(6) SU(2) model with a symmetric external magnetic field and a molecular field approximation, we discover that moderate mixing of Landau levels yields an unexpected re emergence of particle-hole symmetry in the system at moderate mixing strengths, a phenomenon that violates a known theorem. Increasing the temperature leads to a significant reduction in this reemerging symmetry, a contrast to what occurs at low temperatures. Our study reveals that the strong mixing of Landau levels leads to a loss of particle-hole symmetry, while demonstrating that this reemerging symmetry is distinct from the original in the ground state. Additionally, we propose a relationship between the proposed model and a recent experiment involving a 5/2 measurement, asserting that the observed fulfillment of shell-model predictions in this study is a pre-requisite for the reported experimental observations.

A newly proposed paper presents the Thakurta metric, claiming it provides an accurate mathematical representation of cosmological black holes, thus enabling characterization through physical measurements. Conversely, as previously noted in a 2015 study, the Thakurta metric has no physical justification and corresponds to a curved spacetime devoid of mass and energy, characteristic of a Goedel universe with a frozen-in rotation. Furthermore, researchers have developed a complete physical model comprising matter and geodesic lines, allowing for a complete characterization of the spacetime. In contrast to the claims made by the authors, this model does not depict cosmological black holes, but rather a unique variant of the Goedel solution. Consequently, the investigation of primordial black holes using the Thakurta metric is unwarranted and previous findings remain valid.

The complexity of gaseous protoplanetary disks, with their non-uniform texture and composition, may affect the formation of planets. To investigate the impact of density variations, a simulated disk model was created with a fixed structure, and a global 2D simulation was conducted to replicate the spiral arms and other features of protoplanetary disks. A series of point-mass model runs with varying positions and masses was then performed to examine how the presence of these models affected the development of the disk. A world model run of nearly an hour revealed that the density of the models had a significant impact on the formation of planets, especially in a scenario where a super-Jupiter mass object was placed at a distant edge of the simulation area and shown to repel material in its path, and a situation where multiple density variations and point-mass models were present at the same time and shown to trigger the development of planets in a scenario where a terrestrial planet zone existed with conditions suitable for planet formation. A comparison with observations of protoplanetary disks showed some similarities between the results and actual data, and a series of tests revealed the significance of density variations, especially in a scenario where a super-Jupiter mass object in the outer edge of the simulation area prevented the development of planets in a scenario where no density variations were present in the model.

The study of overparameterized models, which pass rigorous tests even with more parameters than variables, remains a prominent area of research. Previous attempts have focused on external limitations, such as data privacy constraints, which lead to overparameterization. This paper explores a unique form of overparameterization arising from computational limitations only, a situation previously overlooked. It is shown that overparameterized models can be constructed without appealing to external limitations like adversarial attacks, by exploiting the computational power of the training process itself. These internal limitations can sometimes be bypassed using simplified models, but not always. A distinct phenomenon is identified where overparameterized models with limited computational power (such as neural networks) can outperform models with similar capacity but less computational power.

In a previous work with G. Pinciroff, we found a lower bound for the measure of bohr sets produced by the sum of two measurable sets in a finite-dimensional vector space. This bound was expressed as the product of the two sets' measures multiplied by a constant dependent on the vector space's dimension. This work expands upon our previous collaboration with G. Pinciroff and provides an alternate proof for the same inequality in an infinite-dimensional abelian group that has a countable basis. Additionally, a similar inequality was developed for the product of two sets in a countably dimensional abelian group that is discrete, with the constant replaced with its binary logarithm. however, a comparable inequality was already established by Bergelson and Ruzsa in a work published in 2004.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths and incorporating new validity inequalities to improve solution quality. A comprehensive computational analysis examines how varying pool sizes affect solution quality across multiple scenarios.

This work explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for e-commerce applications, with a specific focus on knowledge understanding. The proposed KnowMulPN architecture combines vision and text modalities, using a single encoder for both inputs that produces complementary multimodal features. These features are then utilized in three distinct knowledge understanding tasks: product categorization, keyword description, and attribute detection. To bridge the knowledge gap between these tasks, Knowledge Gates are introduced, allowing information to flow between them. Additionally, to mitigate semantic information loss, Non-Significant Feature Elimination modules are proposed to retain vital features while eradicating irrelevant ones. Superior performance is demonstrated through benchmarking on a comprehensive dataset containing over 600000 product images and detailed annotations, comparing results favorably with existing multi-modal pretraining models.

A significant characteristic of neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer's disease is the gradual loss of cognitive function. Understanding the underlying progression from mild cognitive impairment to severe dementia can help researchers and healthcare providers forecast patients' future cognitive decline. So far, the most effective methods for forecasting Alzheimer's progression involve collecting extensive patient data on cognitive performance and imaging scans of the brain, a strategy used in the development of linear forecasting models for cognitive decline and brain structure deterioration. However, little has been done to investigate the change in information content within brain regions over time, partly due to a lack of suitable methods for analyzing brain structure progression. Our work uses a novel approach based on a maximally informative brain representation to create a unique forecasting framework. This method, called Deep InfoMax for Algebraic Connectivity, trains a brain graph with weighted edges using a variational autoencoder, where high connectivity between nodes indicates stronger correlations. Our aim is to show that by analyzing the changes in algebraic connectivity over time, we can quantify the disorder of brain structure and predict patients' progression to severe Alzheimer's disease. Our study focuses on early detection and forecasting, and our results indicate that the proposed method outperforms previous approaches, including statistical models and deep learning models without spatial or functional disorder constraints.

This study proposes a new type of recurrent neural network and a learning method that incorporates interactions between words within a sentence to facilitate deeper semantic understanding. A novel triple recurrent neural network structure is introduced that combines interactions between words within a sentence to facilitate comprehension of semantic relationships. This model is applied to understanding the semantic meaning of a sentence as a whole. Learning is achieved through an end-to-end process guided by datasets of known sentence semantics. Evaluations using multiple datasets demonstrate that this model surpasses existing recurrent neural networks and achieves comparable performance to more advanced models like transformer networks.

The understanding of spin-orbit coupling has advanced significantly in recent years, particularly in systems that are not purely derived from the crystal field and orbital angular momentum. This has led to proposals for manipulating spin information in solid-state systems, including those that rely on the Berry phase mechanism. However, research has shown that in systems with interplay between different degrees of freedom, the effective spin-orbit coupling can be substantially larger than what would be expected based on crystal symmetry alone. This has important implications for the design of quantum devices, including the possibility of utilizing stronger spin-orbit coupling to protect spin qubits from external interference. This work investigates how this enhanced spin-orbit coupling can be interpreted within the framework of a correlated metal model that incorporates local interactions and includes the example of cerium based compounds which exhibit large- spin-orbit coupling and related phenomena such as non-trivial topological properties and non-equilibrium behavior. By exploring these interactions and their effects on the electronic bands, the researchers have found that the spin-orbit coupling can be significant, even in situations that would otherwise be considered as not supporting such a large coupling. This enhanced SPCI is responsible for the emergence of several key properties including the formation of a non-trivial band structure, the creation of surface or interface states with protected properties and the development of complex phase diagrams that include topological states near a quantum critical point where the band structure goes to zero. A new approach for generating gravity-like shadows in the context of conformal fields is proposed, applied specifically to a Klein-Gordon field in de Sitter spacetime. Although a Klein-Gordon field itself lacks particle-like properties, the use of a boundary action and the resulting shadow field exhibits propagation characteristics similar to a massless Klein-Gordon field within a flat spacetime, given a precise condition on its dimension. By adhering to the weak scale mirror symmetry, this field's properties can be made consistent with the gravitational constant and Planck scales. Furthermore, this shadow field possesses a stable behavior under the influence of gravity, thus exhibiting a fixed trajectory in a spacetime background with a cosmological constant. Additionally, this approach allows for a natural generation of massless states, as well as an interpretation of the field's dimension as a measure of interaction strength between particles. A related concept known as Conformal Conductor Ghosts is explored in conjunction with conformal fields theory, also resulting in novel predictions for the gravitational sector.

AI models in medical devices are highly reliant on the data used for training and validation. Typically, a separate, independent dataset, known as a validation set, is employed to assess the performance of these models. This set, which is not used for training, provides an estimate of the model's efficacy. A well-established statistical measure of model performance is accuracy, which can be calculated for individual predictions made on the validation set. This work examines the uncertainty of validation set accuracy as a predictor of model performance in real-world settings, where a significant change in data distribution often occurs. We utilize a non-parametric approach, conformal prediction, to investigate the model's performance under distribution shift. This model can estimate the likelihood of a prediction without assuming a specific statistical model and is suitable for a wide range of machine learning algorithms. We have found that the empirical coverage levels of this conformal prediction model can serve as an indicator of the model's effectiveness in real-world scenarios, even in the presence of significant changes in data distribution. Furthermore, the model enables a statistical comparison of the distributions of validation set accuracy and test-set accuracy, thus quantifying the likelihood that a model will underperform in actual-world applications. This finding is demonstrated through a study of two clinical AI models that classify images of skin lesions as benign or malignant, one of which is trained on a single dataset, while the other is trained on a pair of datasets with different characteristics. We highlight that the models' performances can be significantly impacted by distribution shift

High-fidelity simulations involving atomic details are currently being conducted on covalently bonded materials like proteins and nucleic acids using software such as AMBER and CHARMM. These simulations seek to include representations of chemical bonds, which are influenced by quantum effects but primarily behave according to classical principles. There is an increasing need to accomplish simulations involving multiple atoms like carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen over extended time periods, like several microseconds, through the use of supercomputing infrastructure. However, precise simulations involving accurate time scales often fall short in fulfilling a significant objective of these simulations, which involves the comparison of simulated data against experimental data such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) and ultimately enables theoretical predictions.

This includes the utilization of enhanced sampling techniques like metropolis coupled umbrella sampling (MCUS) aimed at identifying and characterizing distinct conformation types. This method however, only enables the evaluation and examination of conformation types along a defined path, like pulling force curves that contrast with experimental observations, which often exhibit energy landscapes comprising multiple dimensions.

Our study verifies that alternating quantization of ANS entropy encoding, as proposed by Shannon in 1948, remains an efficient method for data compression even with modern coding technologies. This encoding uses two variables - lambda and rho - for each symbol defined within a given probability range. Lambda scales linearly to compress faster, while rho shifts to maintain accuracy, although excessive shifting can reduce compression. A symbol's frequency count determines its position within a binary space, with adjacent symbols having a linear relationship via lambda and rho. When both variables are large, this encoding approximates a uniform distribution, utilizing a binary grid for data compression. A theorem by Cover shows that any coding method has a maximum rate of R for a given symbol probability distribution, and any deviation from this optimal rate represents lost data accuracy. Our investigation assesses the performance loss resulting from combining lambda and rho, and how this loss scales with respect to the total number of symbols in the data set, as well as its relationship to lambda and rho. Through both theoretical analysis and a case study, our findings confirm that this combined loss, measuring the difference between actual and optimal data rates, remains minimal - less than one percent for a data set containing one percent of symbols with non-uniform probabilities, with the remaining symbols having uniform probabilities.

The cement paste's pore liquid plays a pivotal role in the dielectric behavior of concrete, yet its dielectric properties have yet to be accurately represented in existing models used in NDE procedures, such as GPR and DDA. This study sought to measure and model the dielectric characteristics of the pore solution found in cement pastes, focusing on the interactions between water, hydroxide ions, and various types of cement additives. Experimental results revealed the dielectric properties of the pore solution to be influenced significantly by the concentration of hydroxide ions, which increases with the cement paste's moisture levels. Two models, a simplified solution-based approach and a model incorporating hydroxide ion concentration and relative humidity, were developed to predict the dielectric properties of the pore solution. This knowledge can help inform the interpretation of NDE results and pave the way for the refinement of models used in these analyses.

In our initial study, we examined the spectral series of heavy hadronic molecules with a quark-antiquark composition, focusing on their radial and orbital variations. Hadronic molecules, different from conventional hadrons, can still be felt in experiments and emerge as key players in understanding hadron physics. By applying the Fierz Transformation, we accurately separated the interactions related to orbital and spatial arrangements within these molecules, thereby obtaining their S-wave radial excitations. Notably, our work covers the spectral results of the first three radial excitations for $c\bar{c}$ molecules, along with a detailed comparison of the $X(3872)$ spectrum, as observed in experiments. Furthermore, we have included the spectral data of $b\bar{b}$ massive molecules, which for $b\bar{b}$ hadronic molecules, only the $X(6820)$ state is listed as a candidate example within the experimental results available to date. Using the $c\bar{c$ and $b\bar{b}$ molecules' spectral results, we have established a mass prediction model for their radial and spatial variations, expecting that future experiments will discover additional members within these families through the study of mass spectra.

Research into militarily induced uninhabited swarm behavior stems from a threat assessment that treats AI-driven automated decision-making as a fixed binary state. Conversely, existing global research focuses on uncovering the underlying dynamics of such behavior, tied to the development and advancement of unmanned swarm technology. This study, employing a mixed methods approach, utilizes a literature review and sentiment analysis to evaluate the development trajectory of unmanned swarm technology. It is grounded in data from 400 academic publications and 600 news articles, employing Sentiment Analysis and leveraging LaTeX-generated figures. The study's findings reveal the primary drivers of unmounted swarm behavior development to be defence and aerospace sectors, with research linked to the appearance of related terms in these sectors' publication titles. Furthermore, a positive correlation between the development of unmounted swarm behavior and the associated risk, impact and technological difficulty is observed.

The regulations that govern the distribution of baryons in the universe are closely tied to the characteristics of dark matter and are T and ρ-dependent according to the established model. In this study, we have used simulations that incorporate either a cold or a hot form of dark matter and we have used the established formula to calculate how the absorption of light by forests of neutral hydrogen changes in response to variations in the average density of the universe and the temperature of dark matter. We have compared these simulations to the actual data, taking into account different scales and levels of refinement and finding that a scale of about one million kilometers that reflects conditions from the time of reionization, a value of two and a half times the average density of the universe and a relatively narrow range of dark matter temperatures is able to accurately predict the observed distribution of correlations without needing additional parameters. In particular, we found that simulations that included a cold dark matter component resulted in a stronger than observed dispersion in the distribution of correlations at higher scales while simulations that included a hot dark matter component and lower than optimal average density of the universe also failed to match the observed data. In contrast, our preferred model of a cold dark matter at two and a half times the average density of the universe and a relatively narrow range of dark matter temperatures resulted in a significantly better match to the observed data.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where charged beams change their directions of emission. By manipulating the beam using an electron lens, scientists demonstrated the transfer of both transverse and longitudinal beam emittances. The innovation facilitates the creation of complicated beam patterns, essential for an energy front-end upgrade at Fermilab, as well as future high-power accelerators designing a beam with distinct arrival times and shapes.

A crucial capability for AI agents that navigates through real-world urban spaces effectively is predicting the trajectories of other agents. Predicting these trajectories can be challenging, especially due to the constantly changing intentions of moving vehicles. In densely populated areas, understanding the social norms of other agents is essential for avoiding collisions. We present a novel forecasting approach that not only uses past data but also continuously reevaluates the social awareness of moving vehicles based on their actual trajectories. This social-aware reevaluation process occurs in real-time and takes into account the inherent uncertainty of agent intentions. We have successfully implemented this method and seen significant improvements in trajectory prediction accuracy when applied to the Interactions Dataset and the SUMO traffic simulation, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling changing agent intentions and underlying uncertainty.

This study examines the differences between different information-theoretic measures of complexity in the context of Boltzmann Machine models. It investigates the correlations between these measures within a system of an extremely simple nature, where the only relevant factors are the overall and mutual entropies of network nodes. Network architecture and the probability distributions of stochastic nature dictate the relationships between these entropies. Correlations between these measures are shown through calculated covariance coefficients. Distinct differences between these measures are highlighted by contrasting them with the overall number of network connections. Furthermore, the study explores temporal complexity by evaluating the dynamic variability of network characteristics over time using statistical methods such as standard deviation and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. It also applies quantitative optimization techniques to assess the effectiveness of distinct information-theoretic measures of complexity. Finally, the study discusses the potential applications of our findings in the analysis of neural networks.

Researchers have been exploring new methods to enable swarms of robots to interact with humans in a more natural and efficient way. Novel research focuses on incorporating hand gestures as a primary means of interaction between humans and swarms, as this approach is easily understood by humans and robust to interference. A crucial challenge lies in the recognition of hand gestures, which necessitates a solution that strikes a balance between the complexity of the technical methods employed and the level of optimization achieved. A particular issue often arises from solutions that optimize the complexity of the techniques used to some extent, thus compromising the effectiveness of the system. This work presents an innovative, decentralized solution for hand gesture recognition that utilizes Sequential Motion Features and Constant Q Transforms for analysis, as opposed to other prevalent methods. Our solution is based on the Hierarchical Temporally Ordered Graph Match for gesture recognition, which has been extensively tested on the GestureD dataset, yielding exceptional results. A significant achievement of this solution lies in its capacity for efficient computation, which has been further demonstrated to allow real-time interaction between humans and swarms that utilize this solution.

The study aims to develop an efficient technique for fusing deep learning models
to improve the accuracy of classification tasks, particularly for identifying
white blood cells using a limited dataset. A novel method for combining neural
networks involves combining the outputs of two pre-trained models, either by
averaging or weighting their results based on performance. This approach
demonstrates enhanced accuracy compared to using a single model or separating
the data and retraining a new network. Furthermore, we publish a comprehensive
dataset that consists of 6000 image samples, representing four types of blood
cells, which can facilitate research and development in this area.

In our research, we use variational quantum evolution to create an efficient protocol for ground state initialization in the Hubbard model. This method involves gradually transforming the initial state into the target ground state at a controlled pace, with the rate determined by an optimal counter-diabatic driving mechanism. Experiments have shown that this procedure can be effectively implemented on near-term quantum computers with a limited number of qubits. A key advantage of our approach is that it yields a more accurate simulation for a given number of runs compared to other adaptive methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the risk of errors during the process can be quantitatively assessed using techniques from classical decision theory. To validate these findings, we analyzed the target state hybrid density of the Hubbard model with N electrons in a 1D chain, employing Green functions to calculate key properties like their spectral density and resonance transitions. These results not only confirm our theoretical analysis but also highlight the importance of proper sampling to guarantee the accuracy of quantum estimates.

This work introduces a new color image processing technique called color phase shifting (CPS), which achieves fast color transformation from a reference image to a target image through local adjustment of image color temperatures. The proposed method leverages recent advancements in hyperspectral imaging, using pseudo-color images with predefined source and target color temperature profiles to determine the necessary color shift. A key innovation in this technique is its ability to efficiently apply minimal color adjustments, requiring only sub-pixel accuracy. The study evaluates several target color temperatures, assessing their impact on image visual properties. Notably, the results demonstrate to achieve optimal image color similarity by setting the target color temperature close to 5800 K, similar to the standard daylight atmosphere temperature. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed technique involves analyzing its applications in multi-exposure tone mapping, image color correction, and some special effects, showcasing its efficiency and effectiveness.
This note provides a concise formula for the terms of the Taylor expansion of e^a, with a formal proof that they are uniquely derived from an explicit generating function.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, where W. Thurston's geometric classification applies, except for the case where S has a nitely generated fundamental group, we demonstrate the existence of a harmonic harmonic branched cover mapping from a Riemannian manifold (S, d) to a hyperbolic 3-sphere (H^3, h). Furthermore, a corresponding uniformization theorem is proven, which expresses the metric of (S, d) as the pullback of h via this harmonic harmonic branched cover.

I'm pleased to introduce the concept of a compact, versatile research facility, which I'll refer to as an alpha-particle laser-plasma system. This facility combines a high-energy laser, capable of generating a narrow, energetic pepper-pot beam, and a compact ion source, also utilizing an ion laser to constrain the ions within a magnetic field cage. The alpha-particle laser-plasma system, or ALPS, for short, offers an innovative and adaptable setting for conducting pioneering research in photon-photon physics, including the study of linear polarization observables in Compton scattering. Specifically, this facility offers the potential to demonstrate symmetry breaking in QED via observation of a voltage-induced change in the Compton scattering polarization axis, even at very low energies, as well as the potential to make precise measurements of the Compton scattering yield, given a highly focused laser spot and undisturbed plasma.

In the two Higgs doublet model with a type-I or type-II implementation, 
breaking to a symmetric vacuum isn't a stable option, as it's not an energy minimised state. Consequently, the model's vacuum structure needs an adjustment, as it's shifted off this unstable state. Implementing a small breaking parameter, $m_{12}$, while keeping its associated matrix element, $m_{12}$, as a small number, achieves this. The purpose of this procedure is to examine various experimental outcomes without considering constraints related to electroweak precision, as small $m_{12}$ and its associated matrix element aren't constrained by these precision measurements. A study presented in this thesis involves an in-depth analysis of the impact of various particle decays on determining model parameters, particularly when interpreting four body decays involving $B$-mesons. A corresponding computer code based on the two Higgs doublet model is developed and used for this purpose, with its contents merged with another two Higgs doublet model code, ensuring accuracy. Furthermore, the analysis considers how to incorporate this code into another established code, ensuring accuracy.

The main aim of this research is to examine the relationship between data formats, specifically those that follow the RDF data model and XML-based structures defined by XML Schema, with a particular focus on the application of Shape Expressions. The latter is a validation mechanism that leverages a formal verification framework, specifically the Information Item Relating Mechanism (IRI). By analyzing existing methodologies for migrating relational data to RDF datasets, this study aims to identify gaps in current approaches and propose a novel strategy that incorporates Shape Expressions to define constraints. The proposed method is demonstrated through a paradigm example and a formal description using Z notation.

A new software package, pyStoNED, has been created for estimating production functions and measuring productivity in a wide variety of industries and economies. This open-source platform offers a user-friendly set of functions for performing key tasks including identifying the best combination of inputs for maximum output, conducting a comprehensive review of the best possible outcomes given varying input levels, and examining the concept of noise and frontiers in multi-output companies. Users can easily run various types of data analyses, such as data transformation (e.g. with input distance functions), the creation of data visualization plots (e.g. to track trends in efficiency over time), and productivity analysis using established methods like the Gross Domestic Product per Worker model. This software also allows for the analysis of quasi-loss functions, which can provide more accurate results in specific situations, and incorporates a major component of the Space for a Linear Regression model, making it a highly versatile tool for productivity analysis.

In this research, we perform an in-depth analysis of combined data from the Run 2 of the LHC from experiments conducted by ATLAS and CMS, focusing on the statistical power to identify the standard model's Higgs boson in associated top-quark production, where one top quark is fully reconstructed and the other decays into quarks, assuming the standard model's signatura. By utilizing the standard model's likelihood ratio method, we find that our sample of 139/fb of combined data offers a sensitivity of 38.1% efficiency in identifying this particular signature, which serves as a benchmark to compare existing and future data from the LHC. Furthermore, our sample of 300/fb of combined data has an estimated false positive rate of 0.2% and a deviation from the standard model's expected value, which indicates a statistically significant discovery with 5.8 standard deviations. We have compared our results with established searches from the LHC by ATLAS and CMS, where our study yields slightly enhanced sensitivity, especially with larger data sets and the standard model's expected efficiency of 38.1%, which deviates from the standard model's value at 5.8 standard deviations. We have expanded our analysis to explore the standard model's and various alternative models' efficiency ranges, which includes CP-violating models, two Higgs doublet models type II, sterile neutrinos, axions, axion-like particles, scalar leptoquarks, scalar color octets

Recent advancements in deep language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across multiple NLP tasks, leading to increased focus on their application in semantic search technologies. This research explores the utility of large language models as a universal basis for language analysis, assessing their ability to perform well on various tasks using three key criteria: (1) achieving great results in standard evaluation datasets, (2) demonstrating strong results in tasks requiring zero data or minimal supervision, and (3) exhibiting the capacity to adapt to new environments. This work delves into the first criterion by evaluating their capacity for conceptual search and information retrieval, while also investigating the second criterion by examining their capacity for unsupervised and minimal-supervision learning in different language modeling tasks. Furthermore, we establish a dataset called DiaGoal, aimed at advancing the goal-oriented language modeling field; this dataset comprises 1,701 sentences gathered through 434 conversations reflecting a goal, as well as 6,213 sentences writing about a goal. We also introduce DiaGoal-four, a dialectal writing task derived from DiaGoal, aimed at enhancing dialectal language processing. Finally, we analyze the results of our experiments on DiaGoal and DiaGoal-four using four fundamental language models: ELMo, DistilRoBERTa, BERT, and XLNet.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality speech recognition, which can be costly due to licensed models. A significant gap exists in research on improving speech recognition technology for the German language. To address this, we have successfully adapted the Lightning-ONNX framework to deploy German models within Python applications. Our experiments demonstrate that a universally compatible German model can be created by fine-tuning a multilingual English-German model, retaining approximately 97% of the base model's German-English translation performance. Moreover, our analysis shows that fine-tuning a highly accurate, domain-specific English model yields superior results compared to broader, more general domains.

Our investigation of the Be stars within the 30 Doradus galaxy yields several key findings. Firstly, the predicted minimal mass for Be star prototypes is roughly 9.2 solar masses, with our observed prototype Be stars having masses spanning from around 15 to 20 solar masses, suggesting a possible further study of lower-mass Be stars to clarify this pattern. Secondly, the angular sizes of the Be star discs within 30 Doradus appear to be significantly larger than those found in the Be stars within the Milky Way, with certain discs estimated to be as large as 3 astronomical units. Furthermore, the relatively slow rotational speeds of the Be stars within 30 Doradus suggest that they experience less rotational splitting of their spectral lines compared to Be stars in the Milky Way, with specific examples illustrating this phenomenon. Lastly, our comparison of the luminosity ranges of Be stars and B-type stars within 30 Doradus indicates that the Be stars, on average, are only slightly more luminous than their B-type counterparts, in contrast to the steeper trend observed in the Milky Way.

To translate Automated Speech Recognition output into written text, Inverse Text Normalization is utilized. Current approaches to ITN are restricted to the data they've been trained on, which often contains errors, ambiguities, and language specific nuances, making them challenging to expand beyond their initial scope. We propose a novel method to improve ITN performance on unseen data by employing a different approach to natural language processing. Unlike traditional neural network-based ITN models, our method employs a series of text normalisation rules to convert spoken language into written language, and uses a database of examples to estimate unknown events. We demonstrate that this method is more effective than existing solutions at translating speech into written text, particularly in environments where data is limited. Additionally, we showcase the benefits of this method when applied to multiple languages through a series of video demonstrations.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

This study introduces a novel, highly efficient Bayesian inference technique, 
which leverages low-rank kernel tensors to facilitate nearly exchangeable 
tangential kernel sampling. 
The sampling process in TK suffers from high computational costs and autocorrelation 
due to its low convergence rate. 
We analyzed the TK's convergence rate and identified the root cause of these issues. 
To resolve these problems, 
we developed NFTK, a novel method using kernel tensors to facilitate 
exchangeable kernel tensor techniques. 
We validated TK and NFTK on a 1D Gaussian model and a 2D synchrosqueezed linear 
fractional Fourier transform model, 
compiling their numerical results and comparing their performance to established 
methods.

Recent research on non-Hermitian topological phenomena has been prolific, yet mechanisms influencing these phenomena are still somewhat enigmatic. This study discovers a mechanism whereby electron-electron interactions reduce one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological characteristics. We reveal that, in a finite correlation strength, an infinite correlation boundary separates one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological systems from correlated ones lacking topological traits. We establish a scenario where two particles' interactions disrupt the one-dimensional non-Hermitian system's inherent chiral edge states by introducing a finite self-energy within the system's bulk. Consequently, edge states transition from being chiral and movable to localized in a non-interacting, correlated environment. Numerical data validate the theoretical framework, and discussions encompass additional features of edge states, in addition to examining extended systems.

Our current research builds upon previous findings by modifying speaking style
features and increasing the variability in synthetic speech. We've identified a
connection between speech characteristics and the perception of speaker traits.
We recorded extensive data on speaker characteristics, including identity, gender,
age, social identity, and communication style, which we then analyzed for our
corpus of 1,024 public testimonies. Our data shows a significant link between
speakers' identity and their use of communication or replacement words. We've
updated the SPECS speech synthesis framework to allow for the incorporation of
speakers' identity and gender in synthetic speech. Our results show that SPECS
can effectively produce speech that is distinct for various identities and
genders, as perceived by listeners.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses emerge through one-loop and tree-level processes. Utilizing the modular symmetry, we explore the numerical range of the neutrino mixing angle theta_13 and relate it to the light dark matter's interaction rate, which is measured by the direct detection experiment XMASS. As a result, we obtain a constraint on the model's parameter space based on the mixing angle theta13 and dark matter mass m_X. Furthermore, we investigate how neutrino oscillation data may yield information about future jet energy loss measurements in heavy ion collisions.

In triaxial nuclei, the intrinsic axis may fluctuate and display collective behavior.
The Dytman-Guichard limit can be applied to a spectrum derived from a Hamiltonian with a deformation parameter based on the Pauli principle.
By incorporating the concept of a minimal length into the Hamiltonian's deformation parameter, the associated collective motion is studied using the projected quasisymmetry basis.
The Dytman-Guichard limit can be applied to a spectrum derived from a Hamiltonian with a deformation parameter based on the Pauli principle.
Key characteristics of certain triaxial nuclei are reproduced using this method on a microscopic level, including low energy shapes and minimal width corrections to the energy spectrum.
For example, the ground states of nuclei such as $^{120}$Te, $^{122}$Te, and $^{124}$Te exhibit the predicted Y$_1$ multiplet, whereas the first excited states of these nuclei correspond to the $\Delta\gamma$ collective motion.
Significant corrections from the minimal length concept are observed in the low-lying energy spectrum of certain nuclei, such as $^{120}$Te, where the energy decrease amounts to around 35 MeV. 
Limited length corrections also improve the prediction of the Y$_1$ shape parameter in the ground state of $^{124}$Te when compared to experimental results.

This paper outlines a direct construction method for full-length Golay complementary arrays, focusing on non-prime number based arrays. It introduces a concept called partial incomplete pairs and establishes relationships to reduce partial incomplete pairs, resulting in Golay complementary arrays. This technique incorporates numbers with multiple divisors, offering a versatile set of design options for Golay complementary arrays. To showcase its potential, two novel Golay complementary arrays are designed using this method, characterized by arrays of 3240 and 5760 elements, respectively, spanning 16 phases. Furthermore, a computer search revealed that these arrays excel over their counterparts in terms of size.

We present an innovative approach for hyperspectral image change detection in complex urban environments, leveraging its multidimensional spectral and spatial properties. A novel deep convolutional neural network architecture, dubbed DCN, is introduced, specifically designed to handle the vast range of features in hyperspectral images. By incorporating a modular approach within each DCN module, our model distinguishes between diverse feature sets – spectral and spatial – while allowing interactions and fusion of these signals at multiple scales. This approach, featuring 9 DCN modules with tailored filter sizes, demonstrated superior performance on the University campus dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our model exhibits exceptional generalizability, outperforming other approaches even on the Pavia University dataset. Notably, our proposed approach performs change detection without the need for labeled data, making it an effective unsupervised learning method. All associated code will be made accessible via a link on the GitHub repository.

A thorough examination has been carried out to establish a connection between residual entropy and viscosity between molecular fluids and their model partner gases. For this purpose, relative entropies and viscosities of gas and molecular fluid partners were computed through ab initio and classical molecular simulations for 11 non-polar and polar compounds, specifically examining the effects of temperature, density, and molecular structure. An study of the Carnahan-Starling equation's applicability to molecular fluids' density, and an analysis of using pair potential or a higher order theory beyond perturbation theory to predict density and viscosity, were also conducted. Interestingly, this investigation found that using a higher order theory that includes density effects can predict a significant improvement in density predictions, but has minimal effect on viscosity predictions which are largely influenced by two-body collisions. Additionally, this study provides an overview of entropy's correlation with viscosity across various temperatures for gas and molecular fluid partners. An recommendation for the estimation of molecular fluid viscosity based on gas viscosity and molecular fluid residual entropy is also proposed.

A cosmological model is proposed where a universe filled with dark matter and dark energy alternates between periods of geometric inflation. The cycle begins with an almost inflationary state of the universe, caused by dark matter, followed by a transition where dark matter and dark gas (dark matter radiation) densities are equal, after which dark gas becomes the dominant component until dark energy, fueled by dark matter particle mass changes, eventually takes over. This new cosmological model is validated by matching observed values such as the number of baryons, number of photons, number of dark atoms, number of dark particles, number of neutrinos and H0 without using any new parameters. The model also predicts a dark particle mass of approximately 5.6-6.7 eV, a dark particle number density of approximately 1.46 x 10^22 km^-3, a dark particle velocity of approximately 0.15 c, a redshift of approximately 0.8 for the matter radiation equality redshift and a matter density of approximately 0.31.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics, known as Invariant-set theory, asserts that particles original to our universe had random paths that weren't random for us to observe. Despite a 2020 claim of a local realist model for quantum mechanics via Invariant-set theory, proof of this model's existence remained elusive until a purported derivation in July 2021. Nevertheless, a closer examination of this derivation in a hidden-variable setting exposes a critical flaw, and we demonstrate that no local realist model exists using Invariant-set theory.

Automatic keyphrase extraction is a crucial process in helping authors streamline
writing by identifying the central themes of a text. This study introduces a new
neural keyphrase extraction technique, called LightKePE, which is tailored for
deployment on edge devices such as smartphones and tablets. LightKePE combines
a lightweight transformer encoder with a global average pooling mechanism, and
utilizes a novel loss function, the k-ngram ranking loss. We evaluate our
approach using the SciTE and PubMed corpora and compare its performance with
current state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our model achieves comparable or
superior performance while being up to five times more compact and
computationally efficient. As a result, we believe that LightKePE has the
potential to enhance writing assistance on mobile devices.

Using dimer models in two-dimensional statistical systems, we examine various non-relativistic fermion theories by adopting a discrete lattice approach. Beginning with a simple Dirac fermion model on the lattice and then introducing a background gauge field, we explore multiple scenarios, including a vortex-like model in a $2\times2$ theory where non-zero eigenvalues lead to a self-energy deformation. Our analysis focuses on calculating self-energy and dispersion maps as well as their respective radiative parts when applicable. In the absence of a magnetic field, our results show that the relativistic Dirac fermion model features an integer-symmetric momentum contribution, whereas introducing a magnetic field results in a complex momentum structure exhibiting complex oscillations. When considering a dimer-based model of mass where edge sites support mass values of equal strength, our findings show that the former induces a significant self-energy, while the latter exhibits self-energy and zero modes at the vortex. Moreover, our relativistic Dirac fermion model's dispersion structure bears resemblance to the former case, and can be related to a gauge field-controlled transition from a $p$-wave to $p^*$-wave superfluid state.

In various disciplines, linear regression with categorical data is a common technique. However, when dealing with large numbers of categories, this regression often runs into problems with the curse of dimensionality. To overcome this challenge, a powerful regularization technique known as the Group Lasso has been developed. Despite its effectiveness in reducing overfitting in statistical models, it still presents some challenges when applied to categorical data. Our research aims to build on this foundation by addressing two key limitations of the Group Lasso in categorical contexts. First, we wanted to improve upon its tendency to set coefficients to zero entirely, which can sometimes result in inaccurate predictions when the group contains irrelevant but non-harmful categories. Second, we sought to avoid the Group Lasso's reliance on pre-selecting a limited number of groups, which can be a laborious and time-consuming process. To achieve these goals, we have developed two innovative methods: the first relies on a novel regularization technique that encourages an estimate close to zero and positive at the same time, and the second utilizes an original algorithm that selects groups automatically without the need for pre-selection. Our findings from applying these methods to both simulated and actual data suggest that the new approaches significantly outperform existing methods across the board.

The growing interdependence of real-time systems has led to a realization that embedded security breaches can have far-reaching consequences, from destruction of critical data to malicious control of industrial systems. As critical embedded systems integrate with networks, their vulnerability to attacks inevitably increases, with potential harm that can be illustrated by recent cases such as automotive hacking. In response to the escalating need for secure and reliable embedded systems, a proposed solution involves deploying a hypervisor to achieve a high level of system security. In this context, a new hypervisor design, dubbed T-Visor, is presented as a general-purpose solution for executing multiple embedded systems on a single platform with guaranteed timing safety. T-Visor is designed to manage mixed-severity real-time tasks with inherent features like guest-level virtual memory, network, and I/O operations. A key advantage of T-Visor is its ability to provide guest-level encryption, isolation, and malware detection, thus enhancing overall system security. Additionally, T-Visor includes a Malicious Code Detector (MCD) for detecting virtual machines malware. Although previous Malicious Code Detectors have been limited to user-level execution, T-Visor has developed a hybrid approach, running MCD at both user-level and guest-level to enhance detection accuracy. In this research, T-Visor's design is thoroughly reviewed, with a comprehensive analysis of previous Malicious Code Detectors also conducted. A practical scenario and experimental testing have been carried out to validate T-Visor's design

Creating comprehensive 360-degree models from individual images or videos is essential, but standard approaches often struggle with consistent labeling when using image geometry rather than a pre-existing understanding of the environment's layout. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel technique that leverages a predetermined prior on the structure of the environment, enabling more effective image registration for building immersive and spatially accurate panoramic experiences. By integrating novel low-complexity constraints and an adaptive sampling method that searches for optimal configuration more efficiently, our proposed solution outperforms existing methods and showcases its capabilities in setting up a seamless 360-degree viewing experience.

Building on previous work, we have established a theoretical framework for chimeras with uniformly distributed variability, starting with coupled populations of oscillators. In this expanded framework, one population is driven by a fully synchronized master oscillator, while the second is driven by a master oscillator with some level of synchronization error. By adjusting the amount of noise added to the master oscillator's signal, we can create a chimeric state where the two populations coexist and exhibit distinct behaviors.
